note: Cranial muscles are organised by pharyngeal arch of origin. Arch identity, marked by cranial nerve, is the primary homology criterion here and is far more constraining than in the limb: Abdala & Diogo (2010) note that in the head each rhombomeric neural crest population forms both the connective tissue of specific muscles and their attachment sites, so cranial muscle attachment is identity-bound in a way limb attachment is not.

muscles.name: Adductor mandibulae complex
muscles.developmental: First (mandibular) pharyngeal arch mesoderm; connective tissue from mandibular-stream neural crest.
synonyms: the externus, internus and posterior positions (Säve-Söderbergh 1945)

consensus.origin: Lateral and dorsal surfaces of the palatoquadrate or its ossified derivatives — in amniotes, the temporal region of the skull.
consensus.insertion: Medial, dorsal and lateral surfaces of the lower jaw (Meckel's cartilage or the dentary and adjacent bones).
consensus.action: Adducts (closes) the lower jaw. The principal biting muscle in all gnathostomes.
consensus.innervation: Trigeminal nerve (CN V), mandibular division — invariant across Gnathostomata.

occurrences.note: Lampreys have no jaws. Their feeding musculature (velar and lingual apparatus) is not homologous with the gnathostome adductor complex, though some of it is mandibular-arch derived and trigeminal-innervated.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae
occurrences.note: Relatively undivided, giving the plesiomorphic gnathostome condition.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Squalus acanthias, from Huber et al.'s descriptions. From the palatoquadrate onto Meckel's cartilage — the primary jaw adductor in all cartilaginous fishes, with multiple divisions. Both elements are homology groups here: the palatoquadrate is the same record as the amniote quadrate and the mammalian incus, so this row and the mammalian masseter's are visibly on descendants of one bone.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae A1–A3, Aω
occurrences.note: Extensively subdivided in teleosts in correlation with the mobile upper jaw. Jayaram et al. (1983) describe the mandibular and hyoid muscle complexes in three species of the catfish genus Arius and find the myological differences taxonomically informative at species level — a reminder that the subdivision pattern varies below the clade level this dataset records.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae A2 + A2-PVM + pseudotemporalis
occurrences.divisionNote: Ambystoma mexicanum. Three adductors, and the criterion separating two of them is a nerve: the mandibular branch of the trigeminal (CN V3) runs BETWEEN the A2 and the A2-PVM. Worth reading against the pigeon, where Jones et al. find the adductor mandibulae externus lateral to both CN V2 and CN V3 where amniotes usually have it between them — the same nerve, used the same way, giving different answers in two taxa. Ziermann & Diogo note the anterior fibres of the A2-PVM look like part of the pseudotemporalis in both larva and adult.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ambystoma mexicanum, adult (neotenic). The A2 arises from the squamosal and inserts dorsally on the dentary. In the LARVA both ends are different: it arises from the palatoquadrate and the orbital cartilage and inserts on Meckel's cartilage, and during development it swings from vertical to diagonal. The A2-PVM's attachments are given for the larva only — palatoquadrate at the commissura quadrato-cranialis anterior, onto Meckel's cartilage — so they are not scored here. This is a metamorphic shift of attachment inside one species, which is a different thing from the between-species shifts the rest of this dataset diffs.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae externus (pars superficialis, media, profunda), pseudotemporalis, zygomaticomandibularis, adductor mandibulae posterior
occurrences.action: Jaw adduction; the trochlear arrangement redirects the muscle line of action over the otic process.
occurrences.note: Werneburg (2011) resolves this complex into discrete muscular units, each with its own innervation pattern, and supplies an exhaustive synonym list keyed to the historical literature back to Bojanus (1819–21).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Trachemys scripta. Origin: Temporal region — the emarginated or fully roofed temporal skull, with the trochlear redirection over the otic capsule (the turtle-specific pulley). Insertion: Coronar aponeurosis and the medial and dorsal surfaces of the lower jaw. Not yet resolved to skeleton.json ids — this is the source's prose, carried here so it is not mistaken for a scored attachment. Re-attributed from *Trachemys scripta*. Werneburg (2011) does not dissect *Trachemys* — his own specimen is *Emydura subglobosa* (PIMUZ 2009.37) and the seventeen mentions of *Trachemys* in the paper are citations to Poglayen-Neuwall (1953) and Edgeworth. Nine of these rows carried `speciesBasis: "survey"`, which this schema defines as a survey naming an exemplar **for this clade**; the exemplar Werneburg names is a pleurodire, and these rows had been reading as observations of a cryptodire nobody in this corpus examined.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae (levator mandibulae externus, longus, articularis)
occurrences.note: Ascaphus truei, dissected by Johnston (2011) alongside Leiopelma. The innervation pattern — whether branches pass lateral or medial to the trigeminal ganglion — is the criterion the older literature used, and Johnston replaces it with insertion geometry: the components are identified by where they insert into the inverted U on the mandible.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ascaphus truei, two specimens, Johnston (2011). Deliberately sparser than the Leiopelma row beside it. Johnston describes the Ascaphus adductor group as similar in general configuration and then names only the differences: the adductor posterior (articularis) is separate while the rest stays a contiguous block, the origin of the internus does NOT extend as far rostrally on the braincase, and V3 emerges in a different position. Only the braincase origin and the mandibular insertion are therefore asserted here. **"Similar to Leiopelma" is a statement of resemblance, not a second set of observations**, and copying the Leiopelma rows across would manufacture six attachments from one sentence.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae complex (externus, posterior, pseudotemporalis, pterygoideus)
occurrences.divisionNote: Columba livia. Jones et al. resolve four separate adductors, three of them further divided, and they disagree with earlier work on the boundaries: the m. AMEP is separable from the m. adductor mandibulae posterior on both sides of their specimen (contra van Gennip 1986), and the posterior is clearly separate from the pseudotemporalis profundus, unlike the arrangement reported for Columba palumbus. They also record that the homology of the externus partes across amniotes has been questioned outright, which is the same caution Johnston (2011, 2014) raises for this complex.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Columba livia, 242 g adult, from contrast-enhanced CT. The union of the four adductors' attachments; each component's own row carries the detail. Note what is NOT here: the separate postorbital bone is absent in birds, so the postorbital and zygomatic PROCESSES that carry part of the externus origin are recorded on the squamosal rather than on a postorbital element.
occurrences.note: In this specimen the externus lies lateral to both the maxillary (CN V2) and mandibular (CN V3) divisions, and the pseudotemporalis profundus bifurcates around CN V3 near its insertion — the nerve's course through the complex is what the CT dataset adds to the older dissections.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae (continuous block)
occurrences.note: Leiopelma hochstetteri, Johnston's primary animal — four specimens against two of Ascaphus, and the fuller description of the two. The group is a continuous block of muscle with no distinct separation into individual muscles, apart from a plane between the adductor mandibulae posterior and the rest, and a separate lateralis. That is the folded-sheet model's central claim made visible: the components are not separate muscles but named limbs of one sheet, identified by where each inserts into the inverted U around the posterior's insertion.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Leiopelma hochstetteri, four specimens, Johnston (2011). The group is one continuous block here, so these rows are the union of the components he traces through it, and the insertions are the folded U his homology model is built on. Most rostral origin on the dorsal braincase medial to the eye, reaching further forward than in Ascaphus or most other frogs. The longus arises from the parietal region, the convexity of the otic capsule and the crista parotica, passes ventrally and rostrally medial to the processus zygomaticus of the squamosal, and inserts around the APEX of the U on the coronoid area. The externus arises from squamosal and quadrate and inserts as the LATERAL limb of the U. The internus inserts medially in two parts — a rostral tendon just medial to the quadrate-mandibular articulation and a caudal fleshy slip beside it. The adductor posterior runs from the anterior face of the quadrate to the dorsal mandible just rostral to the articulation. No row for the lateralis insertion: Johnston gives its origin on the quadrate and its course lateral to V3 but does not state where it ends.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae anterior + posterior
occurrences.note: Hydrolagus colliei. Anderson's muscle group #1, the one group present and unambiguously homologous in all five gnathostomes he compares.

occurrences.name: Masseter, temporalis, the pterygoids and the tensors
occurrences.action: Elevate the mandible; the lateral pterygoid protracts it and opens the jaw; the pterygoids together produce lateral grinding.
occurrences.innervation: Mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Masseter from the zygomatic arch, temporalis from the temporal fossa, medial and lateral pterygoid from the pterygoid plates and the maxillary tuberosity, all to the mandible. **Four muscles, one nerve, and the nerve is the whole argument.** This record calls trigeminal innervation invariant and the muscle present wherever jaws are — the single most robust cranial homology in Gnathostomata. It also warns that subdivision patterns carry no homology weight on their own and the named parts are frequently non-homologous between clades, which is why the four human muscles are scored as parts of this record and **not** distributed among the `adductor-mandibulae-externus`, `-internus`, `-longus`, `-lateralis` and `-posterior` records. Those carve the sauropsid and anuran complex following Johnston's folded-sheet model, which is not a scheme a human jaw can be fitted into without inventing the fit.
occurrences.divisionNote: The tensors are here on Diogo et al. (2008) Table 1, which derives the tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini from the adductor mandibulae A2-PVM bundle and places them on the adductor row for all five mammals it examines — matching the *Ornithorhynchus* and *Rattus* rows on this record. Gest's tables put both on the mylohyoid instead, which is why they stay `membership: "disputed"` with the other claimant named.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae complex
occurrences.innervation: Mandibular ramus of the trigeminal nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Sphenodon punctatus, Haas (1973), from his own dissections of two specimens — one from the Basel Museum and one from the British Museum (Natural History). **The whole complex converges on a structure that is not bone.** Haas follows Lakjer's criterion throughout: the medialis and profundus are defined by inserting on the lateral and medial faces of the basal aponeurosis (Lakjer's Bodenaponeurose, Poglayen-Neuwall's Binnensehne), which is broadly attached along the dorsal surangular and the lateral articular. The aponeurosis has no element in this skeleton and is carried in prose; without it the three-part division of this record cannot be stated at all.

The components are scored separately on their own records. Haas's arrangement is Luther's and Lakjer's, chosen because it subdivides on the relation to the branches of the trigeminal rather than on topography: externus between the mandibular and maxillary rami, internus between the mandibular and ophthalmic, posterior posterolateral to the mandibular.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae
occurrences.attachmentNote: Timon lepidus, Diogo et al. (2008), Table 1. **This lizard has eleven mandibular muscles against a human's eight**, which is the count that makes their point: the mammalian head is not the elaborated end of the series. The A2-PVM bundle here is the one they derive the mammalian tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini from. **No attachments are scored: this source describes none.**

occurrences.name: Jaw adductors, with a detrahens mandibulae
occurrences.divisionNote: Masseter, temporalis and the detrahens come from adductor mandibulae A2, the pterygoideus medialis from A3'; the two tensors are derived by Diogo et al. from A2-PVM, and are carried as disputed because this dataset also scores them as parts of `intermandibularis`.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus, Diogo et al. (2008), Table 1. **The detrahens mandibulae is present in this animal and in none of the other eight taxa in the table** — not in the lizard, not in the rat, tree-shrew, colugo or human, not in the salamander or either fish. It is a jaw *opener* built out of the adductor mandibulae, so a monotreme opens its mouth partly with an arch-1 muscle where every other mammal here uses the arch-2 digastric alone. Worth setting beside this animal's hind limb, where the same pattern recurs: a caudofemoralis retained, a piriformis never acquired. **No attachments are scored: this source describes none.**

occurrences.name: Mammalian jaw adductors
occurrences.divisionNote: The two tensors are carried as disputed: Diogo et al. derive them from adductor mandibulae A2-PVM, and this dataset also scores them as parts of `intermandibularis`.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Rattus norvegicus, Diogo et al. (2008), Table 1. The same six as a human, and the same six as a colugo and a tree-shrew — **the adductor field is where the mammals in this table agree**, and the intermandibularis is where they do not. The rat is the dataset's only therian on this record other than the human, and it is here to make the human row stop standing for Mammalia. **No attachments are scored: this source describes none.**

occurrences.note: Hagfishes have no jaws. Table 1's row for mandibular muscles other than the intermandibularis is empty for both cyclostomes and begins with the adductor mandibulae A2 at the gnathostome ancestor. *Myxine*'s 24 mandibular muscles are labial, nasal, lingual, dental and velar groups, none of them an adductor.

homology.notes:
**Diogo et al. (2008) derive the mammalian tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini from this complex** — from adductor mandibulae A2-PVM, the bundle they identify in *Latimeria*, *Ambystoma* and *Timon* — where this dataset scores both as parts of `intermandibularis` on the human row. Both fields are mandibular-arch and both take CN V, so nothing about arch identity turns on it; what turns on it is which record holds the muscle. Carried as disputed parts on the rows above and unresolved on either record. See `docs/WORKLIST.md`.

The single most robust cranial homology in Gnathostomata. Trigeminal innervation is invariant, and the muscle is present wherever jaws are. Subdivision patterns vary enormously and carry no homology weight on their own; the individual named parts are frequently non-homologous between clades even when the names match. Johnston (2011, 2014) resolves this complex into a folded sheet whose components are identified by where they insert into an inverted U wrapped around the adductor mandibulae posterior; those components are recorded separately here. Miyashita (2016) sets out the mandibular-confinement hypothesis for the origin of the jaw, which is the background for why cyclostome feeding musculature is not homologised with this complex despite both being trigeminal and mandibular-arch derived.
homology.teaching: Establish CN V = arch 1 = jaw closing first, then show that the mammalian masseter/temporalis split is a rearrangement within an ancient field, not a new muscle system.

correspondences.note: Diogo et al. (2008) Table 1 derives this muscle from the adductor mandibulae A2-PVM bundle they identify in *Latimeria*, *Ambystoma* and *Timon*, and places it on their adductor row for all five mammals they examine. **This dataset now follows them for all three of its mammals.** Gest's tables place it on the mylohyoid instead; that is a single-taxon descriptive source settling no homology across taxa, so under `docs/METHODS.md` the newer comparative treatment governs. The edge is kept because the disagreement is real and Gest's reading should stay findable under his name, not because the assignment is still open.

muscles.name: Intermandibularis
synonyms: M. intermandibularis (Fürbringer 1900; Edgeworth 1907, 1935; Byerly 1925; Oelrich 1956; Langebartel 1968)
M. adductor mandibulae anterior and posterior (Duvernoy 1832)
M. platysma myoides, partim (Hübner 1815; Mivart 1867, 1870; Osawa 1898)

consensus.origin: Medial surface of one mandibular ramus.
consensus.insertion: A midline raphe, or the contralateral ramus.
consensus.action: Raises the floor of the mouth; compresses the buccal cavity. Central to suction feeding and to buccal pumping.

occurrences.name: Intermandibularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Squalus acanthias, from Huber et al.'s descriptions. A thin sheet between the two halves of the lower jaw, right and left portions inserting on the midventral raphe. It elevates the floor of the mouth during feeding and respiration, driving hydraulic transport through the oropharyngeal cavity. **Neither end is skeletal at the midline** — the insertion is raphe, which is why this muscle leaves no correlate.

occurrences.name: Intermandibularis
occurrences.note: Described for Arius by Jayaram et al. (1983), alongside the protractor hyoidei.

occurrences.name: Intermandibularis anterior + posterior
occurrences.divisionNote: Ambystoma mexicanum. Two muscles with a clear gap between them. The anterior is the one muscle in the head whose development is always delayed relative to the others — not visible until the end of stage 38, where the rest of the mandibular arch is already banded muscle cells.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ambystoma mexicanum, adult. The anterior stretches between the most anterior medial faces of the dentary; the posterior runs from the dentary to the median raphe, covering the anterior ventral half of the head. Both meet their contralateral partner in the raphe, and the posterior develops FROM its origin at Meckel's cartilage TOWARD that insertion, its fibres turning from posteromedial to latero-medial by stage 40. Two of the three taxa scored on this record now end at a raphe rather than on bone — the shark in Huber et al. and the pigeon in Jones et al. are the others — so the muscle's medial end is invisible to osteological reconstruction across gnathostomes, not just in one clade.

occurrences.name: Intermandibularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Werneburg resolves a pars principalis and a further unit; both run from the medial dentary to the midline. Re-attributed from *Trachemys scripta*. Werneburg (2011) does not dissect *Trachemys* — his own specimen is *Emydura subglobosa* (PIMUZ 2009.37) and the seventeen mentions of *Trachemys* in the paper are citations to Poglayen-Neuwall (1953) and Edgeworth. Nine of these rows carried `speciesBasis: "survey"`, which this schema defines as a survey naming an exemplar **for this clade**; the exemplar Werneburg names is a pleurodire, and these rows had been reading as observations of a cryptodire nobody in this corpus examined.

occurrences.name: Mylohyoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Columba livia. From the lingual edge of the dorsal ridge of the lower jaw into the median raphe. The same arrangement Huber et al. describe in Squalus: a sheet slung between the two rami whose midline end is a raphe and not a bone. Two of the three taxa now scored on this record insert on a raphe, which is the reason this muscle is invisible to osteological reconstruction at its medial end regardless of clade.

occurrences.name: Intermandibularis
occurrences.note: Hydrolagus colliei. Present in every taxon Anderson (2008) examines, stretching between the sides of the mandible on CN V. In the elasmobranchs it is continuous with the superficial constrictors; in Hydrolagus and the osteichthyans it is separate, which is the topological difference his group #3 has to absorb.

occurrences.name: Mylohyoid and the anterior belly of digastric
occurrences.action: Elevates the floor of the mouth and the hyoid; tensor tympani damps the ossicular chain; tensor veli palatini tenses the soft palate and opens the auditory tube.
occurrences.innervation: Mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). **This record's own assessment says the mammalian derivatives illustrate the point better than any limb example, and this is that row**: a muscle that ends up inside the ear still carries CN V. Mylohyoid keeps the ancestral sheet between the two mandibular rami, meeting its fellow at a midline raphe; the anterior belly of digastric is a strap cut out of the same sheet; tensor veli palatini has moved back into the palate; and tensor tympani has left the mouth altogether to insert on the malleus, scored here as `hyomandibula-stapes`, the middle-ear element group. Four muscles in four unrelated places, one trigeminal nerve, one ancestral sheet.
occurrences.divisionNote: The tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini were parts of this row until Diogo et al. (2008) Table 1 was read against it. They derive both from the adductor mandibulae A2-PVM bundle they identify in *Latimeria*, *Ambystoma* and *Timon*, and place them on their adductor row for all five mammals they examine. **Gest's tables, which put them here, describe one animal and settle no homology across taxa**, so under the rule in `docs/METHODS.md` the newer comparative treatment governs and the two muscles now sit on `adductor-mandibulae`. Nothing about arch identity turns on it — both fields are mandibular-arch and both take CN V — but a student now finds the muscle in one place instead of two.

occurrences.name: M. intermandibularis
occurrences.innervation: Mandibular ramus of the trigeminal nerve; the more posterior transverse fibres by the facial nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Haas (1973), from his own dissections of two specimens — one from the Basel Museum and one from the British Museum (Natural History). A thin transverse sheet joining the mandibular rami, well separated from the sphincter colli behind it — Ruge (1897) figured the two as confluent, which Haas takes to be an error, since Versluys, Wettstein and Poglayen-Neuwall all show a clear gap. **The interesting part is that the sheet is split by nerve, not by shape.** Poglayen-Neuwall found only the oralis, which does not reach the symphysis, to be trigeminal, with the confluent posterior fibres facially innervated and interrupted ventromedially by a rhombic tendinous sheet as the sphincter colli is. Byerly (1925) instead reports a dorsal trigeminal intermandibularis superposed on a parallel ventral facial muscle. Haas records both readings without choosing, and says the muscle shows considerable individual variation. This record already holds the mammalian derivatives — mylohyoid, anterior digastric, tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini — and the tuatara shows the sheet at the point where the trigeminal and facial halves are still in contact.

occurrences.name: Intermandibularis posterior and intermandibularis anterior
occurrences.attachmentNote: Timon lepidus, Diogo et al. (2008), Table 1. Both divisions present under their plain names — the arrangement the mammalian rows have to be read against. **No attachments are scored: this source is a scheme of correspondences and describes none.**

occurrences.name: Mylohyoideus and digastricus anterior
occurrences.divisionNote: Both are intermandibularis **posterior** derivatives. This animal has no intermandibularis anterior.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus, Diogo et al. (2008), Table 1. **The mammalian mylohyoid and anterior digastric are both the posterior intermandibularis** — not the muscle and its anterior partner. Lightoller (1942) describes a mylohyoideus profundus, a mylohyoideus superficialis and, superficial to the latter, a digastricus anterior; Saban (1971) holds that all three come from one embryological structure corresponding to the intermandibularis posterior of other vertebrates, with Jarvik (1963, 1980) in support. Diogo et al. add two independent lines: innervation, since the intermandibularis and the digastricus anterior are both supplied by the ramus ventralis of CN V, and the development of the marsupial *Dasyurus*. **No attachments are scored: this source describes none.**

occurrences.name: Mylohyoid group, with a transversus mandibularis
occurrences.divisionNote: The first two are intermandibularis posterior derivatives; the transversus mandibularis is the intermandibularis **anterior**.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Rattus norvegicus, Diogo et al. (2008), Table 1. **The rat keeps an intermandibularis anterior and the platypus and the human do not** — it is the muscle Greene (1935) called the transversus mandibularis. Diogo et al. are explicit that the rat's mylohyoideus and digastricus anterior correspond to the *posterior* intermandibularis precisely because the transversus mandibularis already holds the anterior position, with Bryant (1945) in support. Across their nine taxa the anterior division survives in *Latimeria*, *Ambystoma*, *Timon*, *Rattus* and *Tupaia* and is gone in *Ornithorhynchus*, *Cynocephalus* and *Homo* — **so it is lost more than once inside Mammalia**, and a human is a poor guide to what a mammal has here. **No attachments are scored: this source describes none.**

occurrences.name: Tubulatus
occurrences.note: Ziermann et al.'s Table 1 puts an **undifferentiated intermandibularis muscle sheet** at the last common ancestor of extant Vertebrata and of extant Cyclostomata, and the tubulatus is what *Myxine* has in that position. It is a long tube-like muscle acting as a constrictor, arising from the lingual arches and surrounding the longitudinalis linguae. The intermandibularis proper — divided into anterior and posterior — appears at the gnathostome ancestor, so this row is the outgroup state the arch-1 ventral sheet is read against, not an intermandibularis in the gnathostome sense.
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Myxine glutinosa*. Scored on `lingual-cartilage`, which is this dataset's element for the hagfish lingual cartilage complex; Ziermann et al. name the origin as the lingual arches. No insertion row — the muscle surrounds the longitudinalis linguae as a tube rather than attaching at a site, and inventing an insertion would be the reader's inference.

occurrences.name: Constrictor cornualis superficialis
occurrences.note: Table 1 places both of these on the undifferentiated intermandibularis sheet of the vertebrate ancestor. *Petromyzon* is credited with 26 mandibular muscles against the hagfish's 24, and none of them is an intermandibularis in the gnathostome sense — that muscle appears at the gnathostome ancestor.
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Petromyzon marinus*, and the rows are the **superficialis only** — Ziermann et al. describe it arising from the cartilago styliformis at the base of the skull and inserting with its contralateral fellow on a median raphe. The profundus internus is named in the table and not described in those terms, so it carries no rows. **The insertion is the point of comparison**: the lamprey muscle meets its opposite number on a midventral raphe exactly as the shark intermandibularis does, so the ventral midline sheet leaves nothing skeletal behind on either side of the jaw origin.

homology.notes:
Present across Gnathostomata with invariant trigeminal innervation. The mammalian derivatives (tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini, anterior digastric) illustrate the point better than any limb example: a muscle that ends up inside the ear still carries CN V.

**Two sources put the tensor tympani and the tensor veli palatini in different fields, and this record has not chosen.** They are scored here as parts of the human mylohyoid row, following the arrangement Gest's tables imply. **Diogo et al. (2008), Table 1, derive both from the adductor mandibulae instead** — specifically from Ad. man. A2-PVM, the same bundle in *Ambystoma*, *Timon* and *Latimeria* — and put them on their adductor row for every mammal they examined. Nothing about arch identity turns on it: both fields are mandibular-arch, both take CN V, and the teaching point about a muscle keeping its nerve into the middle ear survives either way. What turns on it is which record a student finds the tensor tympani under. The disagreement is recorded on `adductor-mandibulae` as well, and is an open decision in `docs/WORKLIST.md`. This record's computed authority, Ziermann & Diogo (2019), is a chapter on **fish** head-muscle development and takes no position on the mammalian question, so the more recent date does not settle it.
homology.teaching: Pair the tensor tympani (CN V, arch 1) with the stapedius (CN VII, arch 2) — two tiny muscles millimetres apart in the middle ear, from different arches, with different nerves. The best available proof that arch identity is durable.

correspondences.note: Held here until Diogo et al. (2008) Table 1 was read against the row. Gest's tables place this muscle on the human mylohyoid; Diogo et al. derive it from adductor mandibulae A2-PVM and this dataset now follows them. Retained as a correspondence so the older reading stays findable. See `adductor-mandibulae`.
