Gest's tables place this muscle on the human mylohyoid; Diogo et al. derive it from adductor mandibulae A2-PVM and this dataset now follows them. Retained as a correspondence so the older reading stays findable. See `adductor-mandibulae`.
Arch 1 and arches 3-7 of the same ventral constrictor series; see the arch-2 edge on `interhyoideus`.

The ventral constrictor series, arch by arch. Diogo et al. (2008) organise their mandibular table into ventral and dorsal blocks explicitly *sensu* Edgeworth (1935), and the ventral member of each arch is what this series holds: the intermandibularis in arch 1, the interhyoideus in arch 2, the constrictores branchiales in arches 3-7. **Serial, not genealogical** — arch 2 is not descended from arch 3.

muscles.name: Depressor mandibulae
synonyms: M. depressor mandibulae (Mivart 1867, 1870; Versluys 1904; Byerly 1925; Haas 1952; Kochva 1962)
M. digastricus (Duvernoy 1832; Sanders 1870, 1874; McKay 1889; Shufeldt 1890; Phisalix 1922)
M. retractor ossis quadrati (d’Alton 1834; Hoffmann 1879-90; Radovanović 1928, 1935)
M. costo-mandibularis / M. neuro-mandibularis (Duvernoy 1832; Owen 1866; Langebartel 1968)

consensus.origin: Posterior skull roof — squamosal, otic region, or the hyomandibula.
consensus.insertion: Retroarticular process of the lower jaw.
consensus.action: Depresses (opens) the lower jaw.

occurrences.name: Constrictor hyoideus dorsalis (levator hyomandibulae)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Squalus acanthias, from Huber et al.'s descriptions. Recorded here as the levator hyomandibulae, which originates on the otic capsule of the chondrocranium and on the epibranchial musculature. The dorsal and ventral hyoid constrictors insert on the tendinous sheath overlying the hyomandibular cartilage, the dorsal arising from the otic capsule and the cucullaris and the ventral alongside the interhyoideus on the raphe of the first gill slit.

occurrences.name: Depressor mandibulae (with levator hyoideus integrated)
occurrences.divisionNote: Ambystoma mexicanum, adult. Scored single because the levator hyoideus is not present as a distinct muscle in the adult — it is integrated into the depressor mandibulae. The ceratomandibularis is the other member of this complex, and its state across urodeles is genuinely variable: a distinct muscle in some obligate neotenes, completely fused to the branchiohyoideus and/or the depressor mandibulae in others, and missing in others again.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ambystoma mexicanum. Two insertions on two different bones, because two muscles fused: the depressor mandibulae proper attaches to Meckel's cartilage in the larva and the dentary in the adult, while at stage 44 some medial fibres of the complex still reach the ceratohyal in a steep angle, which is what makes those recognisable as the levator hyoideus. The otic-capsule origin is the levator hyoideus's — Ziermann & Diogo define that muscle by an origin on the otic capsule and an insertion on the ceratohyal — carried here because the two are one muscle in the adult. The fibre orientations still separate them from stage 43: dorsal fibres more vertical, ventral fibres more diagonal. The branchiohyoideus shares the same anlage and runs from the ceratobranchial around behind the jaw joint to the ceratohyal; it has no record of its own here.

occurrences.name: Depressor mandibulae anterior + posterior
occurrences.divisionNote: Necturus maculosus, adult. Two separate muscles, against ONE in the axolotl on the same record — where the levator hyoideus is integrated into an undivided depressor mandibulae. The names come from the constantly divided depressor of adult bolitoglossine plethodontids, all of which develop directly; Bauer's nomenclatural remarks trace 'depressor mandibulae' back to Humphry (1871), who used it for only the caudal part of the muscle in a metamorphosed Andrias.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Necturus maculosus, adult. The anterior arises along the lateral surface of the upper half of the squamosal and, ventral to that, on the otic capsule — the prootic, the opisthotic and the cartilage between them — inserting on the gonial, some rostrolateral fibres reaching the bone directly and most attaching to a tendon that is continuous with the ceratomandibularis tendon. The posterior arises caudal and medioventral to it on the caudalmost squamosal, the opisthotic and the same cartilage, and inserts through a long broad tendon on the posteromedial gonial; that tendon begins level with the dorsal tip of the ceratohyal and is slightly longer than the belly. TWO EARLIER DESCRIPTIONS ARE CORRECTED HERE AND NEITHER IS SCORED: there are no fibres on the parietal, against Fischer (1864), and no origins on the neck vertebrae, against Ruge (1897). Kesteven (1942-45) also put the whole posterior insertion on the ceratohyal, which Bauer finds among urodeles only in Siren.

occurrences.name: Depressor mandibulae
occurrences.note: Xenopus laevis, the anuran of Ziermann & Diogo's (2013) developmental series. The row previously claimed a leiopelmatid, which that paper does not examine.

occurrences.name: Depressor mandibulae
occurrences.attachmentNote: One to two heads from the caudal, lateral and dorsal squamosal, occasionally the quadrate or quadratojugal; inserts partly by tendon on the posterior and ventral articular and the retroarticular process. Werneburg lists 13 synonyms for this muscle alone. Re-attributed from *Trachemys scripta*. Werneburg (2011) does not dissect *Trachemys* — his own specimen is *Emydura subglobosa* (PIMUZ 2009.37) and the seventeen mentions of *Trachemys* in the paper are citations to Poglayen-Neuwall (1953) and Edgeworth. Nine of these rows carried `speciesBasis: "survey"`, which this schema defines as a survey naming an exemplar **for this clade**; the exemplar Werneburg names is a pleurodire, and these rows had been reading as observations of a cryptodire nobody in this corpus examined.

occurrences.name: Depressor mandibulae
occurrences.attachmentNote: Columba livia. From a broad area on the posterolateral surface of the squamosal, and also from the posterior and lateral surface of the postorbital ligament — a soft-tissue origin that leaves no bony trace. It inserts over a broad continuous area of the lower jaw: the dorsolateral corner, the flat posterior surface, and the posterior end of the medial surface. No landmark is asserted, because that area is wider than the retroarticular process this record's consensus names. Jones et al. add that because the quadrate is mobile, contracting it can protract the upper jaw as well as rotate the lower — one muscle acting on both jaws.

occurrences.name: Posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid
occurrences.action: Elevates the hyoid; with the anterior belly, depresses the mandible.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Posterior belly from the mastoid notch, stylohyoid from the styloid process, both onto the hyoid. **The digastric is two muscles from two arches sharing one tendon**: the anterior belly is trigeminal and is scored on `intermandibularis`, the posterior belly is facial and is scored here. A human jaw opener made by splicing a mandibular-arch muscle to a hyoid-arch one, which no non-mammal does. In other tetrapods this record's muscle runs straight from the skull to the retroarticular process and opens the jaw by itself.

occurrences.name: M. depressor mandibulae
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Haas (1973), from his own dissections of two specimens — one from the Basel Museum and one from the British Museum (Natural History). From the posterior borders of the parietal and squamosal, the post-temporal arcade and the ligamentum nuchae, bypassing the quadrate to insert on the short retroarticular process. **It is a single muscle, and Haas reads that as primitive**: it includes a nuchal component corresponding to the M. cervico-mandibularis, which is a separate muscle in Squamata. A connecting bundle — Lubosch's Verbindungsbündel, which Haas confirms in his own dissections — runs from the nuchal part of this muscle to the medial surface of the anterior end of the sphincter colli aboralis, and he calls the existence of that bundle almost certainly primitive too. Two facial-nerve muscles still physically joined.

occurrences.name: M. depressor mandibulae
occurrences.attachmentNote: Agama stellio, Haas (1973), from his own dissection — his original figures 34, 35, 38 and 40. Figured with a distinct **accessory head**, which Haas labels separately in four of his original figures and which lies deep to the main belly alongside the intermandibularis posterior. Compare the *Sphenodon* row on this record, where the muscle is single and includes the nuchal component that squamates separate off as the cervico-mandibularis — Haas reads the undivided tuatara condition as primitive.

occurrences.name: Depressor mandibulae
occurrences.attachmentNote: Timon lepidus, Diogo et al. (2008), Table 2. One undivided muscle. **This lizard has three hyoid muscles in total** — this one, the cervicomandibularis and the interhyoideus — against a platypus's twelve and a human's twenty-seven. **No attachments are scored: this source describes none.**

occurrences.name: Styloideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus, Diogo et al. (2008), Table 2. **The monotreme styloideus is the reptilian depressor mandibulae**, and so is the therian stylohyoideus that replaces it. Against Edgeworth (1935), who derived both from the interhyoideus, Diogo et al. follow Huber (1930a) and Saban (1968, 1971) — the styloideus of Huber (1930a) is the interhyoideus of Edgeworth and the posterior digastric of Parsons (1898), which is how much of this depends on whose name you are reading. The stapedius comes from the same field and is scored on `stapedius`. **No attachments are scored: this source describes none.**

occurrences.name: Stylohyoideus and digastricus posterior
occurrences.attachmentNote: Rattus norvegicus, Diogo et al. (2008), Table 2. Where the platypus has one muscle from this field the rat has two, and a colugo and a tree-shrew have three — the jugulohyoideus as well. **The digastric is two muscles from two arches with two nerves**, and this record holds the posterior belly while `intermandibularis` holds the anterior: Gasser's (1967) developmental study has the human digastricus posterior, stapedius and stylohyoideus arising from a single anlage, which is this field. **No attachments are scored: this source describes none.**

occurrences.name: Depressor mandibulae
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955); anconal and palmar are dorsal and ventral in their usage. **M. depressor mandibulae.** The extent of the origin from the postero-lateral area of the occipital region and the posterior face of the opisthotic process may be observed in figures 2 and 4. On the lateral surface of the process the origin is tendinous and fleshy, but it goes dorsad as a tendinous apo- neurosis to the level of the deep slip of M. add. mandib. ext. superf. From the most ventral and medial tip of the opisthotic process, a strong tendon forms a major part of the origin of the deeper, medial portion of the muscle; in fact, many of the tendinous fibers pass through the fleshy belly and thus go from origin to insertion and serve as a ligament. MUSCLES OF THE SKULL A *Insertion.* The superficial and most ventral part of the insertion is tendinous on the postero-ventral corner of the lateral surface of the mandible. The primary insertion is fleshy on the entire area of the pos- terior end of the mandible, bordered anteriorly by the posterior end of M. pteryg. vent. (fig. 1).

homology.notes:
Jaw opening is an arch 2 (CN VII) function, jaw closing an arch 1 (CN V) function, throughout Gnathostomata. The digastric preserves both in one named muscle.

**Diogo et al. (2008) trace where this muscle goes in mammals, and it is not one muscle.** Against Edgeworth (1935), who derived the monotreme styloideus and the therian stylohyoideus from the interhyoideus, they follow Huber (1930a) and Saban (1968, 1971): the monotreme **styloideus and stapedius**, and the therian **stylohyoideus, digastricus posterior, jugulohyoideus, stapedius** and possibly mandibulo-auricularis, all correspond to the depressor mandibulae of reptiles such as *Timon*. Gasser's (1967) developmental work supports it from the other end — in modern humans the digastricus posterior, stapedius and stylohyoideus arise from one anlage. So the reptilian jaw opener is the source of a middle-ear muscle, a hyoid suspensor and half a digastric, and the human row on this record holds only part of what the reptilian row holds.
homology.teaching: The digastric is the cleanest single dissection for making the arch system tangible — one muscle, two nerves, two arches, one tendon.

muscles.name: Interhyoideus / constrictor hyoideus ventralis
synonyms: M. constrictor colli (Edgeworth 1907, 1935; Lubosch 1933, 1938; Kochva 1962; Secoy 1971)
M. platysma myoides, partim (Mivart 1867; Sanders 1870, 1874; Osawa 1898)
M. mylohyoideus, partim (Meckel 1821-33; Cuvier 1836-46; Stannius 1856; Hoffmann 1879-90)

consensus.origin: Hyoid arch elements (ceratohyal, hyomandibula) or the associated fascia.
consensus.insertion: Midline raphe of the throat, or the skin.
consensus.action: Constricts the pharyngeal floor; in mammals, moves the facial skin.

occurrences.name: Constrictor hyoideus ventralis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Squalus acanthias, from Huber et al.'s descriptions. A thin sheet lying dorsal to the intermandibularis, from the ceratohyal cartilages of the hyoid arch onto the midventral raphe, elevating the floor of the mouth. The hyoid-arch counterpart of the intermandibularis, and it shares its insertion.

occurrences.name: Interhyoideus (anterior + posterior)
occurrences.divisionNote: Ambystoma mexicanum. A thin anterior and a thicker posterior part whose border is not always clear, which is why this is `heads` and not `divided`. They develop in that order, anterior before posterior.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ambystoma mexicanum, adult. From the ceratohyal to the median raphe. The reason this row matters more than its two elements suggest is Ziermann & Diogo's Fig. 3C: in the adult all the superficial ventral muscles are fused into ONE THIN SHEET, and can only be divided by their origins — the mandible for the intermandibularis posterior, the ceratohyal for the interhyoideus. The attachment is not merely where the muscle ends; here it is the only thing that makes two muscles two.

occurrences.name: Constrictor colli / interhyoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: The constrictor colli complex, six units in Werneburg's scheme. Its spread from the hyoid onto the posterior skull is the sheet that in mammals becomes the facial musculature. Re-attributed from *Trachemys scripta*. Werneburg (2011) does not dissect *Trachemys* — his own specimen is *Emydura subglobosa* (PIMUZ 2009.37) and the seventeen mentions of *Trachemys* in the paper are citations to Poglayen-Neuwall (1953) and Edgeworth. Nine of these rows carried `speciesBasis: "survey"`, which this schema defines as a survey naming an exemplar **for this clade**; the exemplar Werneburg names is a pleurodire, and these rows had been reading as observations of a cryptodire nobody in this corpus examined.

occurrences.name: Serpihyoideus + stylohyoideus
occurrences.divisionNote: Columba livia. Two CN VII bellies from the same hyoid-arch sheet, distinguished by where they end: the serpihyoideus at the midline, the stylohyoideus on the hyoid skeleton.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Columba livia. Serpihyoideus from the posterodorsal surface of the lower jaw to the midline; stylohyoideus from the posterodorsal region of the lower jaw, underlapped medially by the serpihyoideus, onto the lateral surface of the basihyale. The split ends of one sheet are what makes this record's mammalian synonyms — platysma, stylohyoid — legible: the same sheet, ending on skin in one clade and on the hyoid in another.

occurrences.note: No homologous interhyoideus in Hydrolagus colliei, against its presence in the other four gnathostomes Anderson (2008) compares — Amia, Latimeria, Squalus and Chlamydoselachus — so he reads a secondary loss in chimaeroids. Recorded as `no` for this species only; the holocephalan sample here is one animal.

occurrences.name: Facial expression musculature and platysma
occurrences.action: Move the skin of the face, scalp, eyelids and lips; close the eye and the mouth; compress the cheek against the teeth.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). **The single largest expansion of any muscle group in this dataset.** The ancestral interhyoideus is one ventral sheet of the hyoid arch, a constrictor; in a human it has spread over the whole head as some thirty named muscles, and Gest's head and neck table is mostly them. Almost none of them reaches bone at both ends: they arise from the skull and insert into skin, which is what a sphincter sheet does when it stops encircling something. Every one of them is on the facial nerve, which is the only reason they can be recognised as one group at all — the same criterion this dataset uses for the trapezius and the sternocleidomastoid, and for the four trigeminal muscles of the `intermandibularis` row. The listed parts are the principal members, not the full set.

occurrences.name: M. sphincter colli and associated facial muscles

parts.name: Connecting bundle to the depressor mandibulae

occurrences.attachmentNote:
Sphenodon punctatus, Haas (1973), from his own dissections of two specimens — one from the Basel Museum and one from the British Museum (Natural History). Haas lists six facial-nerve muscles for the tuatara: depressor mandibulae, sphincter colli, intermandibularis caudalis, stylohyoideus, ceratohyoideus, and the connecting bundle between the first two. The sphincter colli is divided into oral and aboral portions after Lubosch, the aboral lying posteroventral to the depressor mandibulae.

**Two of these are argued over in ways worth keeping.** Haas holds that Poglayen-Neuwall's M. intermandibularis caudalis cannot be Lubosch's sphincter colli oralis, because the latter crosses the lateral surface of the mandible while the former is the paired posterior continuation of a strictly intermandibular muscle — and suggests either individual variation or that most workers simply missed Lubosch's thin anterior oralis. And the **M. stylohyoideus is found elsewhere among reptiles only in the Gekkota**: it arises at the dorsal end of the hyoid arch and inserts either into the sphincter colli (Ruge) or on the base of cornu branchiale I (Byerly). Byerly considers the ceratohyoideus the anterior belly of a digastric.

occurrences.name: Interhyoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Timon lepidus, Diogo et al. (2008), Table 2. One muscle. **This is the row the whole facial musculature comes out of**: in their scheme a fan of arrows runs from this single lizard muscle to the platypus's interhyoideus profundus, sphincter colli superficialis, cervicalis transversa, orbicularis oculi, buccinatorius, naso-labialis and orbicularis oris, and on into the therian face. **No attachments are scored: this source describes none.**

occurrences.name: Naso-labialis
occurrences.divisionNote: A sphincter colli profundus is recorded in the echidna but not the platypus, so the monotremes disagree with each other here. The platypus's twelve hyoid muscles in Diogo et al.'s count include the styloideus, stapedius, platysma cervicale and platysma myoides, which are dorso-medial and scored on `depressor-mandibulae` and `stapedius` rather than here.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus, Diogo et al. (2008), Table 2. **The platypus already has the core of a mammalian face**: an orbicularis oculi, an orbicularis oris, a buccinatorius and a naso-labialis, plus a dilatator nasi, a maxillo-naso-labialis and a levator anguli oris facialis. What it does not have is the zygomatic group, the auricular group, the mentalis or the procerus. Its twelve hyoid muscles sit between a lizard's three and a rat's twenty-three, which is the sequence this record exists to show — **the mammalian face is built by subdividing one pharyngeal constrictor sheet, and the monotreme is the stage where that is half done.** The platysma cervicale and platysma myoides are derived by Diogo et al. from the reptilian cervicomandibularis rather than from the interhyoideus, so the neck sheet and the face come from two different arch-2 muscles and not one. **No attachments are scored: this source describes none.**
occurrences.note: Reduced to the naso-labialis after the facial split: Table 1 of Diogo et al. (2009) gives *Ornithorhynchus* ten facial muscles, and every one it resolves against the other mammals is now a record of its own. The naso-labialis stays here because Table 1 shows it dividing into the levator labii superioris and its neighbours in the primates, so it is one muscle in the platypus and several in a human, and the correspondence needs the footnotes read before it can be a record.

occurrences.name: Sphincter colli and the facial muscles
occurrences.divisionNote: A partial list: Diogo et al. count twenty-three hyoid muscles in this animal excluding the extrinsic ear muscles, and several of those are dorso-medial and belong on `depressor-mandibulae` and `stapedius`.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Rattus norvegicus, Diogo et al. (2008), Table 2. **Twenty-three hyoid muscles against a lizard's three.** The rat is here because the human row cannot carry Mammalia on this record: a human has twenty-seven and a tree-shrew twenty-five, so the elaboration is therian rather than primate, and Diogo et al.'s own summary is that the facial count rises at the transition to therian mammals and not again at the transition to higher primates. Diogo et al. (2009) resolve the primate end of it muscle by muscle — see that source's reading note for why this record has not yet been split into the fifteen or twenty it would take to hold them. **No attachments are scored: this source describes none.**

occurrences.note: Table 2 credits *Myxine* with four adult hyoid muscles — craniolingualis and craniohyoideus on the constrictores hyoidei of the cyclostome ancestor, and the protractores cartilagines basalis anterior and posterior — and **none of them is the interhyoideus**, which the table first records at the last common ancestor of extant Gnathostomata.

**Table 2 credits *Petromyzon* with no adult hyoid muscles at all** — the column is zero against the hagfish's four. The interhyoideus first appears at the gnathostome ancestor. This absence and the hagfish one together are what make the interhyoideus a gnathostome character rather than a vertebrate one.

occurrences.name: Stylohyoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955); anconal and palmar are dorsal and ventral in their usage. **M. stylohyoideus.** The disto-anterior part of the opisthotic process (fig. 1) gives tendinous origin primarily, while there is strong fleshy and tendinous origin from the middle of the postero-lateral corner of the mandible. Insertion—The fleshy and fascial attachment is to the most antero- lateral surface of the ceratohyal. The anterior end of the insertion is marked by the articulation between the ceratohyal and basihyal bones (fig. 10). *Insertion.* The fleshy and fascial attachment is to the most antero- lateral surface of the ceratohyal. The anterior end of the insertion is marked by the articulation between the ceratohyal and basihyal bones (fig. 10).

homology.notes:
The transformation of a pharyngeal constrictor sheet into the mammalian facial musculature is tracked by constant CN VII innervation. This is arguably the most dramatic functional relocation of any vertebrate muscle field.

**Diogo et al. (2008) route the mammalian facial muscles through this field.** They support Lightoller (1942) and Saban (1971): the reptilian sphincter colli — itself an interhyoideus derivative — corresponds to the mammalian sphincter colli superficialis and profundus and everything descended from them, while the reptilian cervicomandibularis, which runs more obliquely and lies deeper, is a separate matter. They note the older view that the mammalian facial muscles were *de novo* structures has been abandoned. Set against `depressor-mandibulae`, which they read as the source of the stylohyoideus rather than this field, the two records divide the arch-2 musculature of a mammal between them. Diogo et al. (2009) resolve what happens after that: the primate sequence is reshuffling rather than accumulation — strepsirrhines differentiate a depressor supercilii that tree-shrews do not and lack their zygomatico-orbicularis and sphincter colli superficialis; macaques lack the sphincter colli profundus and mandibulo-auricularis but gain six muscles around the mouth and nose; hominoids gain the risorius, auricularis anterior and temporoparietalis while losing the differentiated platysma cervicale that a macaque has. **This record is one row where that is fifteen or twenty**, and splitting it is a live option — see the reading note for why it waits on a descriptive myology of a mammalian head.

**The mammalian facial musculature has been split out.** This record held it as `parts` of one occurrence per taxon — fifteen on *Rattus*, fourteen on *Homo* — where Diogo et al. (2009) Table 1 resolves it muscle by muscle across ten mammals with a proposed unifying nomenclature. Seventeen of those rows are now records of their own, each carrying `descends-from` back to here. What remains on this record is the interhyoideus proper and the parts Table 1 does not resolve into a single mammalian muscle.
homology.teaching: Directly clinically relevant: explains why Bell's palsy affects the whole hemiface plus the stapedius (hyperacusis) but spares chewing (CN V, arch 1).

correspondences.note: The ventral constrictor series, arch by arch. Diogo et al. (2008) organise their mandibular table into ventral and dorsal blocks explicitly *sensu* Edgeworth (1935), and the ventral member of each arch is what this series holds: the intermandibularis in arch 1, the interhyoideus in arch 2, the constrictores branchiales in arches 3-7. **Serial, not genealogical** — arch 2 is not descended from arch 3.

muscles.name: Ceratomandibularis
muscles.developmental: Hyoid arch. Bauer's point is neurological: it is supplied by the facial nerve, which places it in arch 2 with the depressor mandibulae and against the branchial muscles it lies among.

consensus.origin: Anterior surface of the first ceratobranchial.
consensus.insertion: The hyomandibular ligament, and through it the gonial; some fibres to the dorsal ceratohyal and some fused with the depressor mandibulae posterior.
consensus.action: Opens the jaw, pulling the lower jaw down against the hyobranchial apparatus rather than against the skull.

occurrences.name: Ceratomandibularis
occurrences.attachmentNote: Necturus maculosus, adult. Origin on the upper two-thirds of the anterior surface of the first ceratobranchial, sparing the dorsalmost region, dorsal to the ceratohyoideus externus. Most of it inserts onto the HYOMANDIBULAR LIGAMENT together with the depressor mandibulae posterior, and so reaches the gonial only INDIRECTLY — the gonial row is that indirect attachment and the ligament row is the direct one, which is the distinction the two elements exist to keep. Two fibre bundles fuse with the depressor mandibulae posterior outright, and the ventralmost fibres attach to the caudal surface of the upturned dorsal end of the ceratohyal, just above where the ceratohyoideus externus ends.
occurrences.note: Necturus maculosus, adult, and Bauer's contrast is with every urodele larva and with Proteus: in those the ceratomandibularis is simple, while in Necturus it is HIGHLY COMPLEX, partly split by the fascia of origin of the interhyoideus posterior, whose medial layer pierces the muscle. He adds something no earlier worker reported — its deep fibres INTERMINGLE with those of the ceratohyoideus externus in two places, caudally where both attach to the ceratobranchial and rostrally near the posteroventral ceratohyal, while superficially the two are thoroughly separate. A muscle boundary that exists at the surface and not in depth.

Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Not listed. A urodele jaw opener that pulls against the hyobranchial apparatus rather than the skull; the human jaw is opened by the digastric, which pulls against the hyoid but is built from two arches and is scored on `depressor-mandibulae` and `intermandibularis`.

homology.notes:
A jaw opener that pulls against the hyobranchial apparatus rather than the skull, and the reason the urodele jaw-opening system cannot be read as one muscle. Its state across urodeles is genuinely variable: Ziermann & Diogo (2013) report it as a distinct muscle in some obligate neotenes, completely fused to the branchiohyoideus and/or the depressor mandibulae in others, and missing altogether in others — and where it fuses with the depressor mandibulae, the levator hyoideus is fused there too. So an absence in this record may be a loss or may be a fusion, and no source here separates the two for any species but this one.

**`M. ceratomandibularis` is also six authors' name for the geniohyoideus.** Haas's (1973) synonymy list gives it as a synonym of the M. geniohyoideus in Mivart (1867, 1870), Fürbringer (1876), Hoffmann (1879-90), Osawa (1898), Richter (1933) and Langebartel (1968) — a hypobranchial muscle running from the medial mandible to the hyoid arch, on the hypoglossal nerve. This record holds Bauer's (1997) urodele CM, a jaw opener that pulls against the hyobranchial apparatus. The two are not the same muscle and the tuatara is where the usages meet: Haas describes Osawa's *Sphenodon* 'ceratomandibularis' and calls it the geniohyoideus, which is why the tuatara's row for it sits on [[hypobranchial-muscles]] and not here.
homology.openQuestion: Is the ceratomandibularis absent or merely fused in the urodeles reported to lack it? Bauer's fibre-level observation in Necturus — superficial separation with deep intermingling — suggests the question may not have a clean answer at the level of gross dissection.
homology.teaching: The counterexample to 'jaw opening is the depressor mandibulae'. Here two CN VII muscles open the jaw, one from the skull and one from the gill skeleton, and only one of them reaches the jaw directly.

muscles.name: Stapedius / depressor hyomandibulae
muscles.developmental: Second pharyngeal arch mesoderm — the same arch as the stapes/hyomandibula it acts on.

consensus.origin: Otic region / pyramidal eminence.
consensus.insertion: Stapes (or hyomandibula), on its neck.
consensus.action: Damps stapedial movement, attenuating loud sound.

occurrences.name: Depressor hyomandibulae
occurrences.note: Acts on the hyomandibula in its original role as a jaw suspensory element. The animal is Leucoraja erinacea, not the dogfish this row named for several passes: Ziermann et al. describe the muscle only in the little skate, and their discussion of its development from the hyoid condensation is explicitly about batoids. Their Squalus acanthias hyoid section lists an interhyoideus, a constrictor hyoideus dorsalis and an adductor arcus palatini, and no depressor. Whether a selachian has one is a question this source does not answer, so it is not scored as an absence either.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Leucoraja erinacea. Insertion onto the hyomandibula and onto the horizontal tendon associated with it. No origin row — both heads arise from fascia, one at the contact with the contralateral muscle over the coracomandibularis and one on the fascia overlying the sternohyoideus, so the muscle that becomes the mammalian stapedius begins its recorded history attached to the element at one end and to nothing skeletal at the other.

occurrences.name: Stapedius
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). From a pyramidal eminence in the middle-ear wall to the neck of the stapes — **the smallest skeletal muscle in the human body, and one of the most important rows in this dataset for arch identity.** It is the depressor hyomandibulae of a shark, on the same facial nerve, still attached to the same element: this project keeps the hyomandibula and the stapes as one skeletal record precisely so that the shark's muscle and this one do not appear to attach to different bones. Its partner in the ear, tensor tympani, is trigeminal and belongs to the mandibular arch, so the two ossicular muscles are from two different arches and their nerves say so.

occurrences.name: Stapedius
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus, Diogo et al. (2008), Table 2. Present, and grouped by them in the dorso-medial hyoid block with the styloideus — **both are depressor mandibulae derivatives**, following Huber (1930a) and Saban (1968, 1971) against Edgeworth (1935). So the muscle in a monotreme's middle ear and the muscle that opens a lizard's jaw are the same field, which is the muscular half of the argument the `hyomandibula-stapes` element makes with bone. **No attachments are scored: this source describes none.**

occurrences.name: Stapedius
occurrences.attachmentNote: Rattus norvegicus, Diogo et al. (2008), Table 2. Present, as in the platypus, the colugo, the tree-shrew and the human — **the one muscle of this field that every mammal in their table keeps**, while the styloideus, stylohyoideus, jugulohyoideus and digastricus posterior come and go around it. This record previously held a skate and a human and nothing between them.

homology.notes:
The hyomandibula→stapes transformation is one of the best-documented in vertebrate evolution, and the muscle acting on it tracked the element throughout. The spiracular sequence of Gai et al. (2022) is the skeletal counterpart of this muscle's history: the pouch it sits beside becomes the tympanic cavity.

**Diogo et al. (2008) place this muscle in the depressor mandibulae field**, following Huber (1930a) and Saban (1968, 1971) rather than Edgeworth (1935): the mammalian stapedius derives from the levator hyoideus / depressor mandibulae of other tetrapods, and in modern humans it shares an anlage with the digastricus posterior and the stylohyoideus (Gasser 1967). Monotremes have both a stapedius and a styloideus from the same field. That is a developmental argument for what the skeletal record shows independently — this muscle followed the hyomandibula into the middle ear rather than being built there.
homology.teaching: Teach with the tensor tympani. Two middle-ear muscles, two arches, two nerves, both retained through a wholesale change of function.

consensus.origin: Branchial arch elements and the adjacent fascia.
consensus.insertion: Adjacent branchial elements and the midline raphe.
consensus.action: Compress and expand the branchial chamber for gill ventilation; in tetrapods, swallowing and vocalisation.
consensus.innervation: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) for arch 3; vagus nerve (CN X) for arches 4–7.

occurrences.name: Constrictor branchiarum (+ constrictor pharyngis)
occurrences.note: Hagfish branchial musculature is difficult to homologise cell-for-cell with the gnathostome series; Oisi et al. (2013) provide the developmental basis.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Myxine glutinosa, and the row is mostly a record of what is NOT bone. Ziermann et al. give the constrictor branchiarum an origin on the mesentery and insertions onto the connective tissue around the efferent branchial ducts, the surface of the heart, and the fascia of the branchial pouches — not one skeletal attachment among them. Only the anterior fibres, the constrictor pharyngis, reach cartilage: they arise from the lateral tissue of the chorda, which is tissue beside the notochord rather than the notochord itself and so is left unscored, and insert on the lateral borders of the posterior lingual cartilages. A branchial constrictor that ends on the heart and the tongue skeleton is the strongest single argument in this record against reading the hagfish series as the gnathostome one.

occurrences.name: Constrictores branchiales externi
occurrences.attachmentNote: Petromyzon marinus. The muscle is a single external sheet wrapped around the outside of the branchial basket and divided into seven segments by the cartilages and the gill openings, so its attachments are to the longitudinal bars of the basket rather than to any one arch: the fibres run ventrally to the taenia longitudinalis ventralis, and the medial portion lies beneath the epitrematica and hypotrematica. Scored on `taenia-longitudinalis` by side, dorsal for the epitrematica. No origin row — the sheet arises from the basket's own segmental cartilages along its whole length, which is a field rather than a site. External to the gills is the point: the gnathostome constrictors lie inside them.

occurrences.name: Constrictores + levatores arcuum branchialium
occurrences.attachmentNote: Squalus acanthias, from Huber et al.'s descriptions. The superficial branchial constrictors take origin from the tendinous intersections between the dorsal and ventral series and insert on each of the gill slits, compressing the pharynx during the expulsion phase. Scored at the arch and the slit: the tendinous intersections are the real proximal attachment and have no element.

occurrences.name: Branchial musculature
occurrences.note: Lepisosteus osseus, the longnose gar. Naumann et al. trace the development of the branchial muscles and the cucullaris and find they share a cranial mesoderm source. The row previously named a catfish, which they do not examine.

occurrences.name: Dorsal and ventral gill-arch muscles
occurrences.innervation: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) and vagus nerve (CN X).

parts.name: Recti dorsales 1-4
parts.note: Among elopomorphs only Protanguilla has a rectus dorsalis 4 — one of the nine anguilliform synapomorphies this paper identifies.

parts.name: Rectus 4
parts.note: Small in most eels the authors examined but well developed here, and easily mistaken for the R4Cm this species lacks.

occurrences.divisionNote: Protanguilla palau. Fifteen units present, which makes this the most divided this record is in any taxon — the gill basket of a fish against ten units in the axolotl and eight in the pigeon. What is ABSENT matters as much: obliquus dorsalis 3, adductores 1-3, recti 1 and 2, and R4Cm are all recorded absent in this species, and the authors use those absences and presences as characters — nine anguilliform synapomorphies, seven of them myological and all but two reported for the first time.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Protanguilla palau, USNM 396051. The dorsal series: each levator externus arises on the cranium — Springer & Johnson note the exact position was not recorded, which is why the origin row is the neurocranium with no landmark — and inserts on the lateral third of its own epibranchial. The levatores interni insert on the pharyngobranchials, LI2 bifurcating onto Pb3 and the fourth upper pharyngeal toothplate. The recti dorsales run epibranchial to PRECEDING epibranchial, which is the arrangement that needed resolved elements to express at all. RecD1's insertion was lost when the gill arches were removed and is inferred from Anguilla to have been the dorsal tip of the posterior ceratohyal — that is the ceratohyal row, and it is an inference inside an otherwise directly observed set. The ventral series runs ceratobranchial to hypobranchial: ObV1 Cb1 to Hb1, ObV2 Cb2 to Hb2, R3 Cb3 to Hb2, R4 Cb4 to an elongate CARTILAGINOUS Hb3. Ceratobranchial is scored as `cornu-branchiale`, the dataset's record for that element, whose presence list this pass extends to the ray-finned fishes.
occurrences.note: Protanguilla palau. The paper's purpose is phylogenetic — it corroborates anguilliform monophyly and supports Protanguilla as sister to all other eels — so the muscle attachments here are characters first and anatomy second. Two are worth carrying: only this species has a rectus dorsalis 4 among elopomorphs, and a cartilaginous or absent hypobranchial 3 is an anguilliform synapomorphy, that element being largely ossified in all other elopomorphs and most other teleosts.

occurrences.name: Levatores arcuum branchialium I-IV, subarcuales, levatores and depressores branchiarum, transversus ventralis IV
occurrences.innervation: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) and vagus nerve (CN X).
occurrences.divisionNote: Ambystoma mexicanum. Ten units, which makes this the most divided this record is in any taxon and is what a functioning gill apparatus costs. The dorsal levatores develop before the true ventral branchial muscles.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ambystoma mexicanum. The levatores arcuum branchialium I-IV arise from the fascia cephalodorsalis covering the otic capsule, lateral to the epaxial muscles, each inserting on its own ceratobranchial — a fascial origin, so the otic-capsule row is the bone the fascia covers rather than the attachment itself. The ventral series is ceratobranchial-to-ceratobranchial and ceratobranchial-to-hyoid: subarcualis rectus I runs from ceratobranchial I to the ceratohyal in larva and adult alike, subarcualis rectus II-IV from ceratobranchial IV medially onto ceratobranchial I and ventrally onto II and III, and the subarcuales obliqui II and III arise from their own ceratobranchials and fuse before inserting together on the basibranchial. The levatores and depressores branchiarum I-III arise from the commissurae terminales, which are cartilage bars with no element here. Ceratobranchial is scored as `cornu-branchiale` and basibranchial as `corpus-hyoidei`, the dataset's names for those elements.

occurrences.name: Levator + depressor laryngis, constrictor laryngis, dilatator laryngis
occurrences.note: Werneburg (2011) documents the laryngeal muscles as branchial-arch derivatives with distinct innervation.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Re-attributed from *Trachemys scripta*. Werneburg (2011) does not dissect *Trachemys* — his own specimen is *Emydura subglobosa* (PIMUZ 2009.37) and the seventeen mentions of *Trachemys* in the paper are citations to Poglayen-Neuwall (1953) and Edgeworth. Nine of these rows carried `speciesBasis: "survey"`, which this schema defines as a survey naming an exemplar **for this clade**; the exemplar Werneburg names is a pleurodire, and these rows had been reading as observations of a cryptodire nobody in this corpus examined.

occurrences.name: Pharyngeal constrictors, the palatal and laryngeal muscles
occurrences.action: Constrict the pharynx in swallowing; elevate the larynx and pharynx; tense, abduct and adduct the vocal folds.
occurrences.innervation: Vagus (X) through the pharyngeal plexus and the recurrent laryngeal nerve; stylopharyngeus by the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). **The branchial arches after the gills are gone.** Three constrictors wrapping the pharynx onto a midline raphe are the arch constrictors of a fish doing the same job on a different tube; the intrinsic laryngeal muscles are the same series again, reduced to moving three small cartilages. The nerve split is the evidence and Gest records it: stylopharyngeus alone takes the glossopharyngeal nerve, arch three, while everything else takes the vagus, arches four and beyond — so one muscle in the middle of a topologically continuous sheet carries a different cranial nerve because it belongs to a different arch. Cricothyroid takes the external laryngeal branch and the rest take the recurrent laryngeal, which is the second such line drawn inside the same group. **Diogo et al. (2008) find that only one true branchial muscle survives in a human**, and it is the stylopharyngeus — see this record's homology notes and the lizard, platypus and rat rows below.

occurrences.name: Hyobranchialis and 'ceratohyoideus'
occurrences.divisionNote: Diogo et al. read both as a subdivision of the subarcualis rectus I. They quote the lizard 'ceratohyoideus' because it is not the mammalian muscle of that name, and they rename the other muscle hyobranchialis rather than branchiohyoideus because it is not homologous with the salamander hyoid muscle so called.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Timon lepidus, Diogo et al. (2008), Table 3. **Adult lizards lack the branchial muscles sensu stricto as a group** — every one of them except these two. **No attachments are scored: this source describes none.**

occurrences.name: True branchial muscles, three surviving
occurrences.divisionNote: The ceratohyoideus and stylopharyngeus are read by Diogo et al. as a subdivision of the subarcualis rectus I; the subarcualis rectus III is a separate muscle usually present only in adult monotremes.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus, Diogo et al. (2008), Table 3. **The monotreme keeps three true branchial muscles where a human keeps one.** Their summary of the whole series is worth having in full: adult extant mammals lack every branchial muscle sensu stricto except the subarcualis rectus I, present in most adult mammals; the subarcualis rectus II, usually only in marsupials; and the **subarcualis rectus III, usually only in monotremes**. So the three living mammal groups each retain a different member of a series that is otherwise gone, and no one of them shows the mammalian condition. **No attachments are scored: this source describes none.**

occurrences.name: Ceratohyoideus and stylopharyngeus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Rattus norvegicus, Diogo et al. (2008), Table 3. Two, as in a colugo and a tree-shrew; a human has only the stylopharyngeus. **In many mammals, including *Macaca*, the ceratohyoideus and stylopharyngeus are innervated by the same ramus of the glossopharyngeal nerve** — Sprague's buccal ramus — which is the evidence that they are one muscle divided rather than two. **No attachments are scored: this source describes none.**

occurrences.name: Dorsal and ventral gill-arch muscles
occurrences.innervation: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) and vagus nerve (CN X).

parts.name: RecD3
parts.note: Origin slightly ventral to the anterior edge of epibranchial 3, insertion on a well-defined bony process on the posterodorsal margin of ceratobranchial 2, just lateral to mid-length. Springer & Johnson report this attachment as new — Smith & Johnson (2004) figured the muscle without noting it.

parts.name: Ad2
parts.note: Ad1 and Ad2 are Smith & Johnson's (2004) GFM1 and GFM2 reinterpreted and relabelled here.

parts.name: Ad5
parts.note: Dorsally from the epibranchial region with a lateral tendinous attachment to the posterodistal end of ceratobranchial 4; ventrally on the posterodistal half of ceratobranchial 5.

parts.name: LE4
parts.note: Smith & Johnson (2004) show the left LE4 running anteriorly medial to LI1; Springer & Johnson correct this to lateral.

parts.name: TV4
parts.note: On the anteroventromedialmost surface of the ceratobranchial 4 pair, meeting the posteromedialmost edge of R4Cm and underlying the medial end of PCl.

parts.name: TV5
parts.note: Chevron-shaped with a median raphe, attaching laterally to its own ceratobranchial 5 where it meets the ventromedial attachment of Ad5. Only weakly demarcated from the subobliquus behind.

parts.name: PCl
parts.note: Inserts broadly on the ventroposterior surfaces of ceratobranchial 5 and tooth plate 5. Springer & Johnson state that they could not determine **where on the cleithrum** it arises — the bone itself is not in doubt, so the origin is scored as the cleithrum without a side or landmark, which is exactly what an unlocated attachment to a known bone should look like.

parts.name: R4Cm
parts.note: From the ventromedial surface of ceratobranchial 4 beside TV4, forward to the posterodistal edge of hypobranchial 1, attaching there jointly and tendinously with R2. **This is the character that separates Anguilla from Conger**: the same muscle inserts anteriorly on hypobranchial 2 in Conger and on hypobranchial 1 here. Nelson (1967a) did not specify its attachments in Anguilla and said only that the muscles resembled those of Conger.

parts.name: ObV1
parts.note: Tendinous, from the ventromedialmost surface of ceratobranchial 1 to the mid-ventral surface of hypobranchial 1.

parts.name: ObV2
parts.note: Ventromedialmost surface of ceratobranchial 2 to the ventromedialmost surface of hypobranchial 2.

parts.name: ObV3
parts.note: Small, short and weakly developed — Springer & Johnson call it easily overlooked or destroyed in dissection, and completely obscured ventrally by R4 and R4Cm. Ceratobranchial 3 to hypobranchial 3.

parts.name: R2
parts.note: Short and very broad, from the ventroanteromedialmost surface of ceratobranchial 2 to the posterior edge of the hypobranchial 1 – ceratobranchial 1 joint, where it meets R4Cm.

parts.name: R3
parts.note: Ventroanteromedialmost surface of ceratobranchial 3 to hypobranchial 2 ventroposteriorly.

parts.name: R4
parts.note: Ceratobranchial 4 ventroanteromedially to hypobranchial 3 ventrally, its fibres mixing ventrally with those of R4Cm.

parts.name: RecCom
parts.note: **Absent.**

parts.name: SPh
parts.note: **Absent.**

occurrences.attachmentNote: Anguilla rostrata, Springer & Johnson (2015). The second eel column on this record, and the one a student is likely to meet: the American eel against *Protanguilla*, which is hypothesised to be the sister group of all other eels. Ventral muscles described from USNM 190998 (320 mm) with additions from USNM 314441 (296 mm) where muscles were damaged; dorsal muscles from USNM 340815, the descriptions of Smith & Johnson (2004) not repeated except where this paper corrects them. **The ventral series is almost entirely a ceratobranchial-to-hypobranchial system** — every rectus and obliquus ventralis listed runs between those two elements — which is why `ceratobranchials` had to be added to the skeleton for this row; the earlier *Protanguilla* pass added the epibranchials, pharyngobranchials and hypobranchials for the dorsal series and left the ventral limb of the arch with nowhere to attach. PCl's origin is scored on the cleithrum with no side or landmark: the authors could not determine the site on the bone, but the bone is stated, and a coarse attachment beats none.
occurrences.note: Springer & Johnson correct two of Smith & Johnson's (2004) readings of this animal — GFM1 and GFM2 are reinterpreted as Ad1 and Ad2, and the left LE4 runs lateral rather than medial to LI1 — and add an attachment for RecD3 that the earlier account did not note. **Basibranchial 3 varies within the species**: Nelson (1966a) reported it absent in *Anguilla*, and these authors find it absent in a 228 mm specimen, a moderately developed slender cartilaginous rod in a 328 mm specimen, and probably two tiny separated cartilages in two others. That is within-species variation in a skeletal element, recorded here rather than on the element, because it is an observation about these fish.

occurrences.name: Dorsal and ventral gill-arch muscles
occurrences.innervation: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) and vagus nerve (CN X).

parts.name: MUP4-Eb4
parts.note: From upper pharyngeal tooth plate 4 dorso-posterolaterally, becoming a broad thin connective-tissue sheet onto the ventrolateral margin of epibranchial 4 at the angle of its joint with ceratobranchial 4. **Springer & Johnson's one correction to the earlier description**: Smith & Johnson (2004) had it extending medially and becoming incorporated in the sphincter oesophagi, and re-analysis shows it does not.

parts.name: TV5
parts.note: Extends between the distal ends of ceratobranchial 5 on either side. Nelson's 'posterior transversus'.

parts.name: SO
parts.note: Encircles the oesophagus and interconnects the two ceratobranchials 5. Nelson's 'sphincter'.

parts.name: VR
parts.note: **Springer & Johnson disagree with Nelson about whether this is a muscle at all.** Nelson (1967a) illustrated the ventral retractor as a distinct strap, well separated medially from other fibres, attaching to tooth plate 5. They find instead an almost complete sheet of longitudinal fibres, internal to the outer circular layer, attaching on ceratobranchial 5 along the medial edge of the tooth plate, with only a shallow mid-anterior divergence — and say it is a moot point whether to call the longitudinal layer a separate muscle. Not illustrated in their figure: it is entirely hidden by TV5.

parts.name: R4Cm
parts.note: Inserts anteriorly on hypobranchial 2 in this animal, where it reaches hypobranchial 1 in *Anguilla* — the character that separates the two. Springer & Johnson read this out of Nelson's (1967a) own illustration; his text said only that fibres insert on hypobranchial 3 and hypobranchial 2, implying the anteriormost insertion.

occurrences.attachmentNote: Conger cinereus, Springer & Johnson (2015). **A reporting row, and `after` says so.** The dorsal gill-arch muscle descriptions are Smith & Johnson's (2004), from USNM 115969, explicitly not repeated in this paper — Springer & Johnson reproduce the plate and modify exactly one attachment, MUP4-Eb4. What is first-hand here is the ventral musculature figured from USNM 311286, and the re-reading of Nelson's ventral retractor. The row is deliberately thin at the level of individual attachments because this paper does not restate them; the parts carry what it does say.
occurrences.note: Springer & Johnson use this animal mainly as the comparison against which *Anguilla* and *Synaphobranchus* are read, which is why several of its characters appear in those species' sections rather than its own.

occurrences.name: Dorsal and ventral gill-arch muscles
occurrences.innervation: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) and vagus nerve (CN X).

parts.name: LE1
parts.note: Broad, but inserts finely on the medialmost tip of epibranchial 1 together with the anterior end of RecD2.

parts.name: LE2
parts.note: Slender; inserts on epibranchial 2 well medial to the tripartite joint formed by its distal end with the posterior end of pharyngobranchial 2 and the anterior end of pharyngobranchial 3.

parts.name: LE3
parts.note: Inserts on the cartilaginous tip of the levator process of epibranchial 3, which joins a bony process on epibranchial 4.

parts.name: LE4
parts.note: Inserts on epibranchial 4 dorsally, just lateral to mid-length.

parts.name: LE4 prime
parts.note: Less developed than LE4; inserts on the anteroventral edge of epibranchial 4 close to the lateral edge of upper pharyngeal tooth plate 4. **Springer & Johnson flag it as needing verification** and the row keeps that caveat rather than presenting it as established.

parts.name: LI1
parts.note: Inserts broadly along the rod-like portion of pharyngobranchial 2.

parts.name: LI2
parts.note: Inserts on the dorsal surface of the tripartite joint formed by the medial cartilaginous tips of epibranchials 3 and 4 and the posterior cartilaginous tip of pharyngobranchial 3.

parts.name: MPb2-Eb1
parts.note: From the anteromedial corner of the fan-like medial end of pharyngobranchial 2 to the medialmost tip of epibranchial 1.

parts.name: Ad4
parts.note: Originates broadly on epibranchial 4 dorsally and inserts ventrally on ceratobranchial 4 posterolaterally. **The only adductor this animal has.**

parts.name: TD
parts.note: A thin sheet of whitish muscle continuous with the dorsal transverse or circular oesophageal layer, attaching on each side to the posterodistal cartilaginous surface of ceratobranchial 4 and running forward, tapering anteromedially **without attaching to any other gill-arch element**. Springer & Johnson mark it as requiring further study.

parts.name: TPb3
parts.note: The longitudinal oesophageal layer, ventral to the circular one, running forward and somewhat laterally to attach on the medial surface of each pharyngobranchial 3.

parts.name: TUP4
parts.note: Separate, more posterior strands of the same longitudinal layer, attaching to upper pharyngeal tooth plate 4.

parts.name: OD
parts.note: **Apparently absent.**

parts.name: Ad1
parts.note: **Absent.**

parts.name: Ad2
parts.note: **Absent.**

parts.name: Ad3
parts.note: **Absent.**

parts.name: OP
parts.note: **Absent.**

parts.name: RecD1
parts.note: **Absent.**

occurrences.attachmentNote: Serrivomer beanii, Springer & Johnson (2015). **The gill-arch muscles of this animal had never been described or illustrated before this paper.** Tighe (1989) covered much of its osteology and external features and not the muscles. From USNM 315418 (three specimens, about 260, 365 and 545 mm TL) and USNM 383143 (about 590 mm TL). The authors state plainly that the muscles are complex and fragile, that **all specimens were damaged during dissection**, and that the description is a composite of what could be made out across them — so this row is a first description built from several imperfect animals, and should be read as such.
occurrences.note: **Two novelties, both of them absences.** The adductor series is reduced to Ad4 alone, and the obliquus dorsalis, OP and RecD1 are gone. And the epibranchials **completely lack gill filaments**, a condition the authors say they have seen nowhere else. They tie it to a second oddity: the epibranchials are shut out of the branchial chamber by a continuous sheet of black non-muscular tissue that sheathes them — a dorsoanterior extension of the sphincter oesophagi running forward along the whole anterior face of the cleithrum, over the roof of the branchial chamber, then back down onto the posteromedial edge of the fourth arch, the dorsolateral surfaces of the third and second, and much of the dorsal surface of ceratobranchial 1, before continuing into the oral chamber. Not scored as an attachment because it is not muscle.

occurrences.name: Dorsal and ventral gill-arch muscles
occurrences.innervation: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) and vagus nerve (CN X).

parts.name: LE1
parts.note: Inserts broadly and laterally on the dorsoposterior margin of epibranchial 1; its anterior surface is bound tightly to the connective tissue of the roof of the orobranchial chamber.

parts.name: LE2
parts.note: Inserts broadly and laterally on the dorsoposterior margin of epibranchial 2.

parts.name: LE3
parts.note: Inserts narrowly and tendinously on the dorsoposterolateralmost edge of epibranchial 3, and strongly tendinously on epibranchial 4 mid-anterolaterally, almost joining the anterodistal edge of OD4.

parts.name: LE4
parts.note: Inserts on epibranchial 4 from about mid-dorsoposteriorly almost to the lateral end of the bone, meeting Ad4 dorsally.

parts.name: LI1
parts.note: Short; inserts on pharyngobranchial 2 anterolaterally.

parts.name: LI2
parts.note: Inserts broadly on the dorsoposterior surface of pharyngobranchial 3 and onto the posteromedialmost edge of epibranchial 3.

parts.name: TPb3
parts.note: Connects the two pharyngobranchials 3 dorsally, meeting the medial edge of OD4. Its separation from the sphincter oesophagi is marked only by a slight notch either side of its posterior margin.

parts.name: MPb2-Eb1
parts.note: Short; attaches to pharyngobranchial 2 dorsally and epibranchial 1 dorsomedially.

parts.name: OD4
parts.note: Anteriorly on the dorsomedial surface of pharyngobranchial 3, meeting the anterolateral edge of TPb3; posteriorly on epibranchial 4 mid-dorsally, meeting LE3 ventroposteriorly.

parts.name: OP
parts.note: Originates dorsally on epibranchial 4 dorsomedially and the adjacent surface of upper pharyngeal tooth plate 4, meets ER ventrally, and attaches on a tendon joining ceratobranchial 4 posterolaterally to the dorsolateral end of Ad5.

parts.name: DR
parts.note: Originates anteriorly on the dorsolateral surface of tooth plate 4 and the ventromedialmost surface of epibranchial 4, continuing back as the longitudinal layer of the sphincter oesophagi. **Nelson (1967a) first described this muscle and found it in every eel he examined, but did not report that its fibres may also attach to epibranchial 4** — which they do here. Not to be confused with Rosen's (1973) retractor dorsalis, which arises on the anterior vertebrae.

parts.name: Ad1
parts.note: Fan-shaped, spanning the anterior surface of the epibranchial 1 – ceratobranchial 1 joint.

parts.name: Ad2
parts.note: Fan-shaped, spanning the anterior surface of the epibranchial 2 – ceratobranchial 2 joint.

parts.name: Ad3
parts.note: Fan-shaped, spanning the anterior surface of the epibranchial 3 – ceratobranchial 3 joint.

parts.name: Ad4
parts.note: Originates dorsally and broadly on epibranchial 4, meeting LE4, and inserts ventrally on the dorsal surface of ceratobranchial 4, beginning laterally at the inner axil of the joint and extending broadly medially.

parts.name: R4Cm

occurrences.attachmentNote: Simenchelys parasitica, Springer & Johnson (2015). First-hand throughout, from USNM 372009 (about 339 mm TL, Taiwan) and USNM 031727 (about 325 mm, off Massachusetts), with both the dorsal and the ventral series described here rather than referred back to Smith & Johnson (2004) — which makes it, with *Serrivomer*, one of the two eels this paper describes in full. occurrences.note: **All three obliqui ventrales are absent, and the authors offer a functional reason**: the loss is possibly associated with the extremely well-developed ventral gill-arch musculature of this animal. They test it against the closest comparison available — *Synaphobranchus*, whose ventral musculature is much more moderately developed, retains ObV1 and ObV2. That is an absence with a hypothesis attached and a sister taxon to check it against, which is rare in this dataset.

occurrences.name: Dorsal and ventral gill-arch muscles
occurrences.innervation: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) and vagus nerve (CN X).

parts.name: SPh
parts.note: **The dominant muscle of this animal's ventral series, and the reason the others cannot be read separately.** Viewed dorsally it originates broadly on ceratobranchial 4 and attaches anteriorly on the medial end of ceratobranchial 3, dorsal to the anterior attachment of R4; a second portion appears to originate on ceratobranchial 3 and its tooth plate and fuses with the anteromedial edge of the first. The two continue forward, are joined by fibres from hypobranchials 2 and 1, and end on the hypohyal and anterior ceratohyal. It obscures R4Cm, R4 and R3 in dorsal view, all three appearing to fuse dorsally with it and with each other. Springer & Johnson follow Nelson (1967a) in saying that ontogeny, not dissection, will settle what it is made of.

The dorsal muscle descriptions are Smith & Johnson's (2004) and are not repeated in this paper, so this row's attachments are the ventral series only — the dorsal end of the animal is on the earlier source, not this one. **The hyoid attachment is unusual for this record**: the sphincter pharyngis reaches forward past the branchial basket onto the hypohyal and anterior ceratohyal, which is why `ceratohyal` appears among the insertions where the other eels stop at the hypobranchials.
