homology.notes:
Arch-by-arch innervation is preserved from cyclostomes to mammals. The reduction of the posterior arch series in tetrapods leaves the pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles as the surviving remnants of a gill-ventilation system. Higashiyama et al. (2016) document the branchial and intestinal portions of the vagus and their cardiac branches, which is the innervation context for the posterior arch series.

**That last sentence was contested, and this record should say by whom.** Edgeworth (1935) held that the pharyngeal muscles of mammals are *not* derived from branchial muscle plates at all but from a separate *de novo* condensation of myoblasts around the pharyngeal epithelium, and he did not accept that they are homologous with the 'pharyngeal muscles' of amphibians and reptiles. If he were right, the mammalian pharynx would not be a remnant of a gill-ventilation system but a new structure in the same place.

**Diogo et al. (2008) answer him for one muscle, and the argument is from nerves.** Following Smith (1992) and Noden & Francis-West (2006), they hold the stylopharyngeus is not *de novo* but a derivative of the branchial musculature sensu stricto — specifically the subarcualis rectus I. The evidence: the mammalian stylopharyngeus and the reptilian subarcualis rectus I are **among the very few muscles in either animal supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve**, where most mammalian pharyngeal muscles take the vagus; in many mammals including *Macaca* the ceratohyoideus and stylopharyngeus share one ramus of CN IX; and developmental data from **monotremes and marsupials** show the stylopharyngeus early in development resembling the non-mammalian subarcualis rectus I in position, function and connections.

**They stop short of the full claim.** This does not make the mammalian stylopharyngeus the homologue of the reptilian hyobranchialis, because the subdivision of the subarcualis rectus I into two muscles may have happened more than once within Amniota — once giving the lizard's hyobranchialis and 'ceratohyoideus', once the mammal's stylopharyngeus and ceratohyoideus. Settling that needs a comparative analysis across more amniotes and, they say, the fossils. The rows below are scored on their reading; Edgeworth's is recorded here rather than deleted.

**Adult extant mammals keep almost none of this series**, and which one they keep differs by group: the subarcualis rectus I in most mammals, the subarcualis rectus II usually only in marsupials, the subarcualis rectus III usually only in monotremes. A human retains, seemingly, the stylopharyngeus alone.

**The amniote pharyngeal and laryngeal musculature has been split out.** This record held it as `parts` of one occurrence per taxon, where Diogo et al. (2008) Table 3 resolves the branchial, pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles across nine sarcopterygians from *Latimeria* to *Homo*. Eighteen of its rows are now records, each carrying `descends-from` back to here.

**What remains is deliberate.** The cyclostome, chondrichthyan, actinopterygian and amphibian rows keep their parts, because there the muscles are segmental series — levatores arcuum branchialium I–IV, subarcuales recti, obliqui ventrales — rather than named individuals, and Table 3 treats them as a group. **The turtle keeps all four of its laryngeal parts because Table 3 has no turtle column**; splitting them would attribute to that source a taxon it does not examine. And the human keeps the cricopharyngeus and the aryepiglottic and thyroepiglottic, which Table 3 does not list.
homology.teaching: The stylopharyngeus is a memorable single fact: one muscle, one nerve, one arch, the last of its kind.

muscles.name: Extraocular muscles
muscles.developmental: Prechordal plate and cranial paraxial mesoderm — NOT pharyngeal arch derived. Distinct from every other cranial muscle group in origin.
synonyms: rectus superior / inferior / medialis (internus, nasalis) / lateralis (externus)

consensus.origin: Around the optic foramen and the orbital wall.
consensus.insertion: Sclera of the eyeball.
consensus.action: Rotate the eye about three axes; retractor bulbi withdraws the globe.
consensus.innervation: Oculomotor (CN III): rectus superior, inferior, medialis, obliquus inferior, levator palpebrae. Trochlear (CN IV): obliquus superior. Abducens (CN VI): rectus lateralis, retractor bulbi.

occurrences.note: Myxine glutinosa has no extraocular muscles at all, and no ocular motor neurons to supply them — on Fritzsch's compilation the only vertebrate group of which that is true. The eyes themselves are reduced. This is an absence with a mechanism rather than a failure to find the muscle, which is what makes it scoreable as `no` rather than left unrecorded, and it is the floor of the record: lampreys already have six.

occurrences.name: Extraocular muscles
occurrences.note: Petromyzon marinus has a full set of six extraocular muscles on three nerves, establishing that the system predates jaws. The assignments are not the gnathostome ones: three on CN III, one on CN IV, two on CN VI, with a caudal rectus that gnathostomes lose and no medial rectus, which is a tetrapod and coelacanth addition. Sourced to Fritzsch, not to Ziermann et al. — that paper contains no extraocular content and was cited here in error.

occurrences.name: Extraocular muscles
occurrences.innervation: CN III, IV and CN VI, but not the crown-osteichthyan pattern.
occurrences.note: Squalus acanthias, and the chondrichthyan set is neither the lamprey's nor the tetrapod's. Fritzsch gives elasmobranchs and lungfish a contralateral nasal rectus on a dorsal ramus of CN III that crown osteichthyans lack, and no medial rectus; the caudal rectus of lampreys is already gone. The earlier reading of this row as 'the standard gnathostome pattern' flattened two differences in both directions.

occurrences.name: Rectus superior, inferior, anterior, posterior; obliquus superior, inferior; retractor bulbi; ciliaris; sphincter and dilatator pupillae; transversalis oculi
occurrences.innervation: CN III for rectus anterior, inferior, superior, obliquus inferior, ciliaris, dilatator and sphincter pupillae, transversalis oculi; CN IV for obliquus superior.
occurrences.note: Werneburg (2011) records ten distinct ocular muscular units in turtles, including intraocular muscles absent from most vertebrate accounts. Turtles (like birds) have striated intraocular muscles, so pupillary control is partly voluntary.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Eight units around the optic foramen and the anterodorsal optic cavity, all inserting on the eyeball. Werneburg additionally records intraocular muscles (ciliaris, sphincter and dilatator pupillae, transversalis oculi) that most vertebrate accounts omit; turtles, like birds, have striated intraocular muscle. Re-attributed from *Trachemys scripta*. Werneburg (2011) does not dissect *Trachemys* — his own specimen is *Emydura subglobosa* (PIMUZ 2009.37) and the seventeen mentions of *Trachemys* in the paper are citations to Poglayen-Neuwall (1953) and Edgeworth. Nine of these rows carried `speciesBasis: "survey"`, which this schema defines as a survey naming an exemplar **for this clade**; the exemplar Werneburg names is a pleurodire, and these rows had been reading as observations of a cryptodire nobody in this corpus examined.
occurrences.divisionNote: No division recorded, because the two statements on this row disagree: the name enumerates eleven units and the note quotes Werneburg (2011) recording ten. Reconcile against the source before asserting a count.

occurrences.name: Four recti, two obliqui, three levatores palpebrae, pyramidalis and quadratus
occurrences.innervation: Oculomotor (CN III), trochlear (CN IV) and abducens (CN VI).

parts.name: Levator palpebrae obliquus
parts.note: Jones et al.'s survey of columbiform accounts has it present in some and absent or unreported in others.

occurrences.divisionNote: Columba livia. The recti and obliqui are the conserved six; what is added in birds is the nictitating-membrane apparatus (pyramidalis and quadratus) and up to three levatores palpebrae. The retractor bulbi, which this record notes for mammals, is not among them.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Columba livia. The recti arise from a thickened periorbital membrane around the orbital wall and insert on the sclera by quadrant — dorsalis posterodorsal, ventralis anteroventral, medialis anterodorsal, lateralis posteroventral. The obliqui arise from the anterior and anterodorsal orbital wall. The periorbital membrane is worth noting: several of these origins are on connective tissue rather than bone, so the orbit rows are the bony frame of the origin and not the origin itself.

occurrences.name: Extraocular muscles and levator palpebrae superioris

parts.name: Superior, inferior, medial and lateral rectus

occurrences.action: Rotate the eyeball about three axes; levator palpebrae raises the upper eyelid.
occurrences.innervation: Oculomotor nerve (III), except superior oblique (trochlear, IV) and lateral rectus (abducens, VI).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Four recti and two obliques from the common tendinous ring and the orbital wall onto the sclera. **The three-nerve pattern is the most conserved arrangement in the vertebrate head** — one muscle to the trochlear nerve, one to the abducens, the rest to the oculomotor — and it is identical in a lamprey, a shark and a human, which is why this record's development field reads prechordal/somitomeric rather than branchiomeric. What a human lacks is the retractor bulbi, present in most tetrapods on the abducens; levator palpebrae superioris is scored as a fourth part and is the addition going the other way.

homology.notes: The most conserved muscle group in the vertebrate head: same six muscles, same three nerves, from lampreys to mammals. Their non-branchiomeric origin makes them the exception that defines the arch system — they are the cranial muscles that are not arch muscles. Fritzsch (2023) adds the one mammalian wrinkle: the retractor bulbi is retained in many mammals and lost in humans and other primates, so the six-muscle count is a primate simplification of a seven-muscle plan.
homology.teaching: Use as the control case. If cranial muscle homology were merely a matter of position, the extraocular muscles would not be so much more stable than the arch muscles; their stability is a consequence of a developmentally distinct and functionally rigid system.
homology.caveat: Fritzsch (2023) is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed. Cite the primary sources it points to rather than the preprint itself.

muscles.name: Hypobranchial muscles
muscles.developmental: Occipital and anterior trunk somites. The myoblasts migrate forward beneath the pharynx, which is why they are somitic muscles in a cranial position — and why the hypoglossal nerve, a spinal nerve in origin, ends up cranial.
synonyms: M. geniohyoideus (Meckel 1821-33; Owen 1866; Camp 1923; Byerly 1925; George 1948)
M. ceratomandibularis (Mivart 1867, 1870; Fürbringer 1876; Osawa 1898; Richter 1933; Langebartel 1968)
M. genioglossus (Meckel 1821-33; Owen 1866; Camp 1923; Oelrich 1956; Langebartel 1968)

consensus.origin: Pectoral girdle (coracoid/sternum) and the hyoid.
consensus.insertion: Hyoid, mandible and the tongue.
consensus.action: Depress the hyoid and the lower jaw; protrude and shape the tongue. In fishes, expand the buccal cavity for suction feeding.
consensus.innervation: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) and the ansa cervicalis (C1–C3) — spinal in origin, not branchiomeric.

occurrences.name: Hypobranchial musculature
occurrences.note: Present in Petromyzon marinus but with a different arrangement; the lamprey lingual apparatus is not homologous to the gnathostome tongue. Left unscored deliberately rather than for want of a pass: Ziermann et al. describe the obliquus and decussatus as ending on a median raphe and on their contralateral partners, the rectus as continuous with the sphincter cloacae, and the hypobranchialis as a segmented muscle continuous with the parietalis behind and the subocularis in front. Not one skeletal attachment in the set. Where the shark's hypobranchial series runs from the coracoid bar to the mandible, hyoid and branchial arches, the lamprey's runs muscle-to-muscle, and copying the shark's rows here would assert an observation nobody made.

occurrences.name: Coracomandibularis, coracohyoideus, coracobranchialis
occurrences.action: Depress the jaw and hyoid, expanding the orobranchial chamber for suction feeding.
occurrences.innervation: Ventral rami of the occipital and anterior spinal nerves.
occurrences.note: The coracoid origin makes the mechanical link between the pectoral girdle and the feeding apparatus explicit — the same link that must be broken for a neck to evolve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Origin on the coracoid bar ties the feeding apparatus mechanically to the pectoral girdle. Loosening that link is a precondition for a neck.

occurrences.name: Geniohyoideus, sternohyoideus, omohyoideus
occurrences.innervation: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) and the cervical spinal nerves.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ambystoma mexicanum. The geniohyoideus develops from its origin at the basibranchial toward its insertion on Meckel's cartilage and/or the dentary, close to the origin of the intermandibularis anterior; in the adult it widens and closes the gap between the contralateral pair. The sternohyoideus is blended posteriorly with the RECTUS ABDOMINIS — the clearest statement in the corpus that this group is trunk muscle that migrated forward — and inserts on the hypobranchial, dorsally on the basibranchial and medially on the rostral end of ceratobranchial I. The omohyoideus derives ontogenetically from the sternohyoideus, stays deeply blended with it, and extends posterolaterally to the pectoral girdle, which is the girdle end of the link whose loosening Diogo & Ziermann tie to the origin of the neck.

occurrences.name: Geniohyoideus, coracohyoideus, genioglossus, hyoglossus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Aggregated across eight units (genioglossus, geniohyoideus, coracohyoideus, hyoglossus and their parts). Werneburg records CN XII for these, confirming their somitic rather than branchiomeric origin. Re-attributed from *Trachemys scripta*. Werneburg (2011) does not dissect *Trachemys* — his own specimen is *Emydura subglobosa* (PIMUZ 2009.37) and the seventeen mentions of *Trachemys* in the paper are citations to Poglayen-Neuwall (1953) and Edgeworth. Nine of these rows carried `speciesBasis: "survey"`, which this schema defines as a survey naming an exemplar **for this clade**; the exemplar Werneburg names is a pleurodire, and these rows had been reading as observations of a cryptodire nobody in this corpus examined.

occurrences.name: Genioglossus, hypoglossus, cricohyoideus, sternohyoideus, branchiomandibularis
occurrences.innervation: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) and the cervical spinal nerves.
occurrences.divisionNote: Columba livia. Eight bellies, which is the most divided this record is in any taxon. Jones et al. treat the ceratohyoideus with the throat series; it is included here as a part rather than given its own row because no source in this dataset separates it as a homology group.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Columba livia. The tongue and throat series, running between the mandible, the tongue skeleton and the sternum: genioglossus anterior from near the mandibular symphysis onto the floor of the mouth; hypoglossus rectus from the ventral paraglossum onto the anterior entoglossum, obliquus from the ventral edge of the paraglossum; cricohyoideus and sternohyoideus both onto the posterior paraglossum and the dorsal hyoid, the latter from the sternum. The sternal origin is the point of comparison with the shark, where the same field arises from the coracoid bar: what loosened that girdle-to-tongue link is what allowed a neck.
occurrences.note: Somitic rather than branchiomeric, which is what CN XII records.

occurrences.name: Coracomandibularis + coracohyoideus + mandibulohyoideus
occurrences.note: Hydrolagus colliei, and the record's most interesting column. Anderson (2008) finds a coracomandibularis in all five gnathostomes and argues from it that basal jaw depression was NOT coupled to hyoid movement but worked directly through this muscle — the osteichthyan coracohyoideus-through-mandibulohyoid-ligament system being the derived arrangement. He also renames a Hydrolagus muscle called geniohyoideus by some authors and interhyoideus by others to `mandibulohyoideus`, because it matches neither and is apomorphic. Its consequence is that Hydrolagus has TWO ways to depress the jaw, the chondrichthyan coracomandibularis and a geniohyoideus-like mandibulohyoideus, which Anderson raises as possible independent acquisition of an osteichthyan-style depression in chimaeroids.

occurrences.name: Coracomandibularis + coracohyoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Callorhinchus milii. A very large coracomandibularis with its main origin on the T-shaped anteroventral face of the coracoid region of the pectoral girdle, inserting along Meckel's cartilage — triangular in ventral view, broadening forwards. This is the muscle Anderson (2008) finds in all five gnathostomes he compares and argues from: basal jaw depression pulled on the mandible directly from the girdle, and was not coupled to the hyoid. Scoring it here puts the same attachment in a holocephalan and a selachian.

occurrences.name: Infrahyoid, suprahyoid and tongue musculature
occurrences.action: Depress and fix the hyoid and larynx; protrude, retract and change the shape of the tongue.
occurrences.innervation: Hypoglossal nerve (XII) to the tongue and geniohyoid; ansa cervicalis to the infrahyoid strap muscles; palatoglossus by the vagus (X).
occurrences.attachmentNote: Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). **A muscle group that walked forward from the shoulder into the mouth, and its nerve is the receipt.** These are trunk muscles: hypobranchial myotome that migrated under the pharynx carrying the hypoglossal nerve and the ansa cervicalis with it, which is why the tongue of a human is supplied by a nerve that leaves the skull and comes back. Gest's list preserves the whole gradient — sternohyoid and omohyoid still reach the sternum and the scapula, geniohyoid stops at the mandible, and the intrinsic tongue muscles have no bony attachment at all. Palatoglossus is scored as a disputed part: it is in the tongue and named with the tongue muscles, but it takes the vagus and belongs with the palatal muscles on `branchial-constrictors`.

occurrences.name: Hypobranchial and lingual musculature
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Haas (1973), from his own dissections of two specimens — one from the Basel Museum and one from the British Museum (Natural History). Three deep hypobranchial muscles, noted briefly because Haas defers the hyoid-associated musculature to another chapter in the series. Geniohyoideus from the medial mandible near the symphysis to the anterior margin of the medial half of the hyoid arch, leaving its anterior and posterior quarters bare; genioglossus from near the symphysis, dorsal to it, entering the ventrolateral tongue, its most ventral fibres reaching the processus entoglossus and its internal portion — the M. basihyalis proprius — forming circular fibres there that protrude the tongue; hyoglossus from the anterior border of the hyoid arch into the whole length of the tongue. **Haas records that Osawa (1898) called the geniohyoideus a M. ceratomandibularis**, which is a name this dataset holds as a separate record for a urodele jaw opener. The same word, two muscles, and the tuatara is where they cross.

occurrences.name: Geniohyoid and rectus cervicis groups
occurrences.divisionNote: Diogo et al. sort the series into Edgeworth's two groups — 'geniohyoideus' and 'rectus cervicis'. The first three parts here are the geniohyoideus group, the last two the rectus cervicis group.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Timon lepidus, Diogo et al. (2008), Table 4. **No well-developed independent intrinsic tongue muscles are counted for any taxon in this table** — the counts in its header all read 'not in. to.' — but amniotes have them and extant amphibians such as salamanders do not (Piatt 1938, Saban 1968, 1971). Edgeworth (1935) reads the hyoglossus of lizards such as *Timon* as corresponding to part of the coracomandibularis of amphibians and sarcopterygian fish. **No attachments are scored: this source describes none.**

occurrences.name: Geniohyoid and rectus cervicis groups
occurrences.divisionNote: Six, excluding the intrinsic tongue muscles. No styloglossus and no palatoglossus — see the note.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus, Diogo et al. (2008), Table 4. **The therian styloglossus and palatoglossus come out of the monotreme hyoglossus.** Their own dissections support Edgeworth's (1935) suggestion that those two therian muscles likely correspond to part of the hyoglossus of monotremes — so this animal has one muscle where a human has three, and the difference is a subdivision rather than an acquisition. That bears directly on this record's existing note about the palatoglossus being the only 'tongue' muscle on CN X: if it is a piece of the hyoglossus, its vagal supply is harder to explain than a clean arch-4 origin would make it, and Piekarski & Olsson (2007) report that in mammals such as dogs the tongue muscles are sometimes innervated by **both** the hypoglossal and the facial nerve, which they take to indicate a dual origin in at least some cases. **No attachments are scored: this source describes none.**

occurrences.name: Geniohyoid and rectus cervicis groups
occurrences.divisionNote: Eight, excluding the intrinsic tongue muscles. **No palatoglossus** — seemingly not an independent muscle in the rats Diogo et al. dissected, which Barrow & Capecchi (1999) support; a human and a colugo have one and a tree-shrew does not.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Rattus norvegicus, Diogo et al. (2008), Table 4. Greene (1935) did not describe a genioglossus in the rat; Diogo et al. found it as an independent structure in every rat they dissected, with Bryant (1945) reporting it effectively often present in rodents. **This is the group that grows steadily rather than in a jump**: *Latimeria* and *Lepidosiren* have two, *Ambystoma* six, *Timon* five, the platypus six, this animal eight, a human nine — unlike the hyoid muscles on `interhyoideus`, which go from three in a lizard to twenty-seven in a human. **No attachments are scored: this source describes none.**

occurrences.name: Geniohyoideus, genioglossus and the hypoglossi
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955); anconal and palmar are dorsal and ventral in their usage. **M. geniohyoideus.** There is fleshy origin from the entire circumference of the tongue geniohyoideus ceratohyal esophagus trachea Fic. 9. Dorsal view of the tongue and the floor of the pharynx. The stippled area represents a cut edge of the wall. MUSCLES OF THE TONGUE REGION 29 epibranchial cartilage and from the dorsal and lateral surfaces of the posterior half of the length of the ceratohyal. Because of the variab *Insertion.* From the anterior end of its origin the muscle goes ante- riorly and somewhat laterally to insert fleshily on the inner surface of the mandible. This attachment is opposite the basihyal, or about 7 centi- meters anterior to the posterior end of the mandible. The anterior end of the insertion is marked by the most anterior end of the insertion of M. add. mandib. medius on the lateral surface of the mandible. **M. genioglossus.** There is a fleshy origin from the inner side of the mandible, dorsal to the middle of the width of the mandible. The site of the origin is dorsal to the mandibular attachment of M. geniohy. Insertion—From this relatively short and narrow line of origin the muscle fans out as it goes ventro-mediad. homology.notes: The hypobranchial muscles are somitic muscles in the head, and this is exactly what CN XII records — it is a fused series of occipital spinal nerves, not a true cranial nerve of the branchiomeric type. Diogo & Ziermann (2015) connect the loosening of the coracoid-to-mandible link with the origin of the vertebrate neck. Two mammalian details, previously carried by a row attributed to a cheetah that no source dissected: the palatoglossus is the exception that confirms the rule, being the only 'tongue' muscle on CN X because it is a soft-palate (arch 4) muscle rather than a hypobranchial one; and with the coracoid gone the infrahyoid muscles take origin from sternum, clavicle and scapula instead.
homology.teaching: Answers a question students always have: why does a nerve numbered among the twelve cranial nerves behave like a spinal nerve? Because it is one.

muscles.name: Levator arcus palatini / spiracular musculature
muscles.developmental: First pharyngeal arch mesoderm, dorsal division.
synonyms: M. levator pterygoidei (Lakjer 1926; Edgeworth 1935; Oelrich 1956; Kochva 1962)
M. protractor pterygoidei (Versluys 1904; Lakjer 1926; Edgeworth 1935; Oelrich 1956)
M. pterygo-sphenoidalis anterior / posterior (Hager 1905; Adams 1919; Radovanović 1928, 1935)
M. tensor and laxator tympani, partim (Sanders 1870, 1874)
M. levator bulbi, dorsalis and ventralis (Lakjer 1926; Lubosch 1938; Oelrich 1956)
M. depressor palpebrae inferioris (Hoffmann 1879-90; Bradley 1903; Edgeworth 1907, 1935)
M. retractor vomeris (Lakjer 1926; Edgeworth 1935; Albright & Nelson 1959a)

consensus.origin: Otic and postorbital region of the neurocranium.
consensus.insertion: Palatoquadrate or its derivatives; the spiracular region.
consensus.action: Elevates and abducts the palatoquadrate; controls the spiracle where one is present.

occurrences.name: Levator palatoquadrati, spiracularis
occurrences.note: The spiracle is the reduced first (mandibular) gill slit; its musculature is arch 1 and trigeminal.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Squalus acanthias, from Huber et al.'s descriptions. Two muscles on this record. The levator palatoquadrati runs from the otic capsule of the chondrocranium onto the palatoquadrate, elevating the upper jaw into its resting position during the recovery phase of the gape cycle. The spiracularis inserts on the spiracular cartilage and the distal hyomandibula, forming the anterior wall of the spiracular valve.

occurrences.name: Levator arcus palatini, dilatator operculi
occurrences.action: Abducts the suspensorium during suction feeding.

occurrences.name: Protractor pterygoidei et quadrati
occurrences.note: Columba livia. Scored on this record as the amniote representative of the mandibular-arch dorsal division — the muscle that moves the palatoquadrate. The record's other rows are the shark's levator palatoquadrati and spiracularis and a catfish's; this is its first amniote row, and the identification rests on position and on CN V innervation rather than on any source here stating the homology outright, which is why it is worth saying so.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Columba livia. From the posterior surface of the orbit, dividing into two heads: the dorsal inserts on the dorsal edge and posterior surface of the anteromedial process of the quadrate, the ventral onto the posterior surface of the pterygoid. Contraction protracts the pterygoid-quadrate-maxillopalatine complex and opens the UPPER jaw — the cranial kinesis that has no counterpart in the taxa this record's other rows come from.

occurrences.note: Absent in Hydrolagus colliei, and Anderson (2008) gives the reason rather than the fact: the holocephalan palatoquadrate is fused to the cranium (autostylic suspension), so there is no free element to levate. He reads it as a secondary loss — the muscle is basal for gnathostomes and went when the joint did. This is the cleanest case in the dataset of a muscle disappearing because its skeletal degree of freedom disappeared, and the counterpart of the coracoid loss that moves the therian supracoracoideus.

Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). Not listed. The spiracular series has no muscle in a human — but the region does survive: the spiracular pouch is the ancestor of the tympanic cavity, so the space this muscle worked in became the middle ear. The two muscles a human does have in that cavity, tensor tympani and stapedius, come from the mandibular and hyoid arches respectively and are scored on `intermandibularis` and `stapedius`.

occurrences.name: Constrictor internus dorsalis group
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Sphenodon punctatus, Haas (1973), from his own dissections of two specimens — one from the Basel Museum and one from the British Museum (Natural History). **The most variable muscles in the animal, and Haas says so plainly.** The whole group is reduced, as in akinetic or nearly akinetic lizards, and the published descriptions disagree so completely that he attributes the differences to a wide range of individual variation rather than to error. Lakjer is internally inconsistent — his text denies the M. levator pterygoidei exists in *Sphenodon* while his figure shows and labels one.

**M. protractor pterygoidei is present in one specimen and absent in the other**, in Haas's dissections as in Ostrom's (1962); Adams and Poglayen-Neuwall emphatically denied it exists, Versluys, Edgeworth and Lakjer reported it. Haas offers an explanation worth recording: the variation may be ontogenetic rather than taxonomic — juveniles with a more kinetic skull retaining a functional protractor, adults with an akinetic skull losing it. It is scored as a `variable` part for that reason.

The levator bulbi is the exception, well developed and subdivided into dorsal and ventral portions. The ventralis arises from the anterior edge of the orbitosphenoid cartilage and ends on the palatal membrane; the very thin dorsalis arises tendinously from the anteromedial epipterygoid — definitely not from the membranous braincase wall as Poglayen-Neuwall described — carries an internal tendon where it meets the posteroventral eyeball, and **turns dorsally to insert in the lower eyelid**. A rostral portion arises from the palatine in the Basel specimen and the pterygoid in the London one. Scored on this record because the constrictor internus dorsalis group is the amniote descendant of the spiracular/levator arcus palatini series, not on `extraocular-muscles`, which is prechordal and carries the oculomotor, trochlear and abducens muscles.

occurrences.name: Constrictor internus dorsalis group
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Varanus varius, Haas (1973). **A synthesis, not one dissection** — Haas lists himself with Lightoller (1939) and Frazzetta (1962) and says the account rests on all of them together. The narrow levator pterygoidei lies medial to the epipterygoid, from the descending process of the parietal to the pterygoid, raising it anterior and medial to the prootic wing. **The protractor pterygoidei is much larger and here it actually protracts** the palatopterygoid series, arising from the anteroventral process of the prootic, the body and basipterygoid process of the basisphenoid and even the quadrate — the contrast this record needs, because in *Sphenodon* the same muscle is feebly developed or altogether missing and Haas scores it as a `variable` part there. A kinetic skull that uses the muscle, beside an akinetic one that has nearly lost it.

The levator bulbi is complex and subdivided, though Haas notes Bradley (1903) reported only one such muscle in *V. salvator* and Frazzetta (1962) figured only one: a dorsalis functioning as the depressor palpebrae inferioris and inserting along the lower eyelid, and a ventralis functioning as a tensor of the palatal membrane.

occurrences.name: Dorsal mandibular muscles
occurrences.attachmentNote: Timon lepidus, Diogo et al. (2008), Table 1, dorsal mandibular block. Three muscles here, against none in any of the five mammals they examined. Their caption is careful about the levator bulbi: the overall analysis makes the urodele one a dorsal mandibular muscle, **but they cannot completely rule out that it derives from the adductor mandibulae**, and it is drawn with a grey arrow on that reading rather than a black one. **No attachments are scored: this source describes none.**

occurrences.name: Dorsal mandibular muscles
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ornithorhynchus anatinus. **Absent.** Diogo et al. (2008), Table 1, score the whole dorsal mandibular block — levator arcus palatini and its derivatives, the levator and protractor pterygoidei and the levator bulbi — as empty in every mammal they examined: the platypus, the rat, the colugo, the tree-shrew and the human. Set against the lizard row above, which has three, this is a field lost at or before the origin of mammals rather than reduced within them.

occurrences.name: Dorsal mandibular muscles
occurrences.attachmentNote: Rattus norvegicus. **Absent**, on the same table row as the platypus, the colugo, the tree-shrew and the human. The dorsal mandibular muscles move the palatoquadrate and its derivatives against the braincase; in a mammal the quadrate has become an ear ossicle and the upper jaw is fused to the skull, so there is nothing left for the field to move.

occurrences.note: Table 1 first records the levator arcus palatini at the gnathostome ancestor. The cyclostome candidate is the **velar muscle** group — in *Myxine* the craniovelaris anterior dorsalis and ventralis, spinovelaris and craniovelaris posterior — on the hypothesis that the velar muscles and the levator arcus palatini both derive from the constrictor dorsalis anlage that also yields the elasmobranch spiracularis. **Ziermann et al. do not accept it.** The evidence offered is engrailed immunoactivity shared between the lamprey larval velothyroideus and the zebrafish levator arcus palatini (Holland et al. 1993), and they remain cautious about proposing a homologue on immunoactivity alone, noting that engrailed is expressed in gnathostome mandibular myoblasts outside the dorsal mandibular musculature. Scored absent on their reading, with the alternative recorded here rather than deleted.

As for *Myxine*. The lamprey velar muscles — protractor veli, depressor veli and the levator valvulae velaris — are the candidate, and the engrailed argument for homologising the larval velothyroideus with the gnathostome levator arcus palatini is the evidence Ziermann et al. decline to rest a homology on.

occurrences.name: Protractor pterygoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955); anconal and palmar are dorsal and ventral in their usage. **M. protractor pterygoideus.** tThe posterior end of the belly arises, primarily as fleshy fibers MUSCLES OF THE SKULL AND JAWS 25 with a few superficial tendinous fibers interposed, from the most lateral protuberance of the basitemporal plate, which point lies at the level of the posterior end of the quadrate. Insertion.—There is a fleshy insertion, with some superficial fascial connection, on the medial and dorsal surfaces of the anterior third of the length of the pterygoid bone. *Insertion.* There is a fleshy insertion, with some superficial fascial connection, on the medial and dorsal surfaces of the anterior third of the length of the pterygoid bone.

homology.notes:
The spiracular series is important for the origin of the tetrapod middle ear: the spiracular pouch is the ancestor of the tympanic cavity, and the mandibular-arch identity of the region is preserved by trigeminal innervation. Gai et al. (2022) trace the spiracular region from jawless fishes to tetrapods, which is the fossil evidence behind treating the spiracular pouch as antecedent to the tympanic cavity — a claim this record previously made without a source.

Distribution, as the sources give it: present in chondrichthyans and osteichthyans, and probably lost in holocephalans, which Ziermann & Diogo (2019) relate to the fusion of the palatoquadrate with the neurocranium in that clade (after Ziermann et al. 2014; Miyake et al. 1992; Anderson 2008). **No source here states the muscle's fate in mammals.** This record carried a *present: "no"* row for Acinonyx jubatus with no source and a guessed species, reasoning from suspensorium-to-braincase fusion — which is the holocephalan argument transplanted to a mammal by nobody in particular. The row is gone: an unobserved absence is unrecorded, not observed. Didier (1987), a holocephalan myology thesis already in `papers/`, is the way to turn the chimaera loss into a species-level row.
homology.teaching: Connects jaw suspension, gill slits and the middle ear in one developmental field.

muscles.name: Adductor mandibulae internus
muscles.subregion: mandibular arch — adductor complex, medial limb of the U
synonyms: M. pterygoideus internus (Osawa 1898; Sanders 1870, 1874; Hoffmann 1879-90; Edgeworth 1907)

consensus.origin: Dorsal braincase medial to the orbit, and the pterygoid.
consensus.insertion: Mandible, medial to its articulation with the quadrate; via a flat tendon in anurans.
consensus.action: Adducts the mandible; the medial limb of the adductor sheet.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae internus (medial division)
occurrences.note: Callorhinchus milii, the holocephalan in Johnston's comparative material — his model of the adductor complex as a folded sheet was tested from chondrichthyans to mammals, and this is the cartilaginous fish he tested it on. The medial division is identified by where it inserts into the inverted U on the mandible.

occurrences.name: Pseudotemporalis
occurrences.divisionNote: Ambystoma mexicanum, adult. ONE undivided muscle, and that is the result rather than the starting point: the larva has a pseudotemporalis superficialis (the A3' of fishes) and a pseudotemporalis profundus (the A3''), the profundus visible from stage 39, and during larval development it becomes completely integrated into the main body of the muscle. A division event running backwards.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ambystoma mexicanum, adult. The origin has MOVED DORSALLY during development — dorsolateral on the palatoquadrate (orbital cartilage) in the larva, and in the adult from the midline of the parietal and caudally from the first vertebrae. That is a jaw muscle acquiring an axial origin, and it is why this row carries a vertebral element. Insertion caudodorsal on the dentary; in the larva both portions insert on Meckel's cartilage.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae internus (rostral + caudal parts)
occurrences.note: Two parts merging into one another. Johnston prefers 'adductor mandibulae' to 'levator mandibulae' for anurans, to align with usage across gnathostomes.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae internus / pseudotemporalis + pterygoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ctenosaura pectinata. Left unscored, and not for want of looking. Johnston (2014) does not dissect Ctenosaura — his specimens are ten snakes plus Sphenodon punctatus, and his Ctenosaura figure is redrawn **after Oelrich (1956)**, chosen because the absent ventral temporal arch makes the illustration clearer. Even his Sphenodon account reports findings 'as presented in Daza et al. (2011)'. The primary source for iguanid jaw adductor attachments is therefore Oelrich (1956), which is not in the corpus. Johnston remains the right citation for the folded-sheet homology this record's division rests on; he is not a source for where the muscle attaches in this animal.
occurrences.note: **Haas (1973) does not close this row either.** His list of forms studied marks his own animals 'Haas, this chapter' — *Sphenodon punctatus*, *Agama stellio*, *Varanus varius*, *Lanthanotus borneensis* and a *Maticora*. Against *Ctenosaura pectinata* he gives Oelrich (1956) and Avery & Tanner (1971). So the second source in this corpus to describe this animal's jaw muscles is reading the same primary that `docs/GAPS.md` §7 already records Johnston (2014) as reading. **Oelrich (1956) remains the acquisition this row needs**, and two independent checks now say so.

occurrences.name: Pseudotemporalis + pterygoideus

parts.name: Pseudotemporalis
parts.note: Separates a superficial from a deep head in turtles; the superficial head connects through a long intermediate tendon to the intramandibularis.

parts.name: Pterygoideus
parts.note: Origin from the walls of the bony groove or canal linking the lower temporal fossa to the orbit, bordered by pterygoid, palatine, parietal (descending process) and frontal. In pleurodires with a trochlear process a Pars ventro-lateralis arises from its free end, and in Podocnemis a third part arises from the quadrate within a widened canalis carotis internus.

parts.name: Intramandibularis
parts.note: Lies in the Meckelian canal medial to the mandibular nerve, arising broadly from the lateral surface of Meckel's cartilage and running dorsally to the same intermediate tendon.

occurrences.attachmentNote: Testudines, generalised, from Schumacher (1973) with Werneburg (2011). **Not a species observation, and deliberately filed as one that is not.** Schumacher examined roughly forty chelonian species including *Pseudemys scripta*, but writes the synthesis — 'in all turtles X, and in (Emys, Hardella, Testudo, trionychids) Y' — so these rows describe the chelonian condition and its named variants, not an animal. That is the same shape as Werneburg's appendix, and the second turtle cranial source to land on this record. **The turtle CRANIAL column is generalised while the turtle FORELIMB column is now scored to *Trachemys* from Walker (1973)** — one clade, two halves of one skull-and-limb dataset, resting on different kinds of evidence, and the interface now says so on every row.
occurrences.divisionNote: Schumacher treats the internus of turtles and crocodilians as a complex rather than a muscle: a pseudotemporalis plus a pterygoideus, the latter further split into anterior and posterior parts in crocodilians. The intramandibularis is what makes the group unusual — a division of the adductor complex that lies inside the lower jaw.

occurrences.name: Pseudotemporalis + pterygoideus
occurrences.divisionNote: Columba livia. Four bellies in two pairs. This record holds both the pseudotemporalis and the pterygoideus because both are internal adductors of one field — the same grouping Werneburg (2011) uses for turtles.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Columba livia. Pseudotemporalis superficialis has a broad fleshy origin on the posterior wall of the orbit and inserts by aponeurosis at a narrow point on the lower jaw; profundus arises from a small region on the medialmost end of the medial process of the quadrate and inserts broadly on the lateral, dorsal and medial surfaces of the jaw anterior to the coronoid process, taking in most of the adductor fossa — and it bifurcates around CN V3 close to its insertion, which is how the nerve reaches the Meckelian groove. Pterygoideus dorsalis arises from the dorsolateral palatine (anterior part) and the lateral pterygoid (medial and posterior parts); Jones et al. see no part of the anterior head on the pterygoid, against Bhattacharyya. Pterygoideus ventralis arises from the posterolateral ventral palatine and the ventral pterygoid and inserts on the medial surface and posterolateral corner of the jaw. It matters most at large gapes — continuously active during drinking, and during the grasping phase of feeding.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae internus (rostral + caudal parts)
occurrences.attachmentNote: Leiopelma hochstetteri, Johnston's primary animal — four specimens against two of Ascaphus, and the fuller description of the two. The rostral origin on the dorsal braincase medial to the eye extends further forward than in Ascaphus truei or in most other frogs, which is the species difference this row exists to hold — it had been carried as prose on the Ascaphus row. The rostral part converges on a flat tendon inserting immediately medial to the quadrate–mandibular articulation; the caudal part has a more ventral fibre direction and a fleshy insertion on the medial mandible beside that tendon.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae internus (pseudotemporalis + pterygoideus anterior et posterior)
occurrences.action: Adducts the lower jaw; the dominant adductor mass in crocodylians.

parts.name: Pseudotemporalis
parts.note: Inserts on the broad dorsal surface of the mandibular adductor tendon; its own pseudotemporal tendon attaches to the Cartilago transiliens.

parts.name: Pterygoideus anterior
parts.note: Fibres attach to the Lamina anterior of the mandibular adductor tendon, which lies horizontally in the roof of the mouth.

parts.name: Pterygoideus posterior
parts.note: Works through six tendon aponeuroses whose origins and attachments alternate between the base of the skull and the lower jaw.

occurrences.divisionNote: **Greatly developed in crocodylians relative to turtles**, and the reason Schumacher treats the internus as a system rather than a muscle. The pterygoideus is split into anterior and posterior here, which it is not in turtles.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Alligator mississippiensis, Schumacher's own specimen (marked S in his species list). Schumacher's crocodylian tendon system is the point of this column. The **mandibular adductor tendon** (Lakjer's stem tendon) is the insertion for ALL adductors: its main part attaches to the dorsomedial face of the angular, its Lamina anterior lies horizontally in the roof of the mouth, its Lamina posterior spreads from the angular and articular, and its lateral edge reaches the dorsomedial surangular at the coronoid tuberosity — a roughness visible on macerated bone, so an osteological correlate. A **Cartilago transiliens** glides between that tendon and the surangular. The muscles attach to tendon laminae rather than directly to bone, and the rows below therefore name the bone each lamina is anchored on.

occurrences.name: M. adductor mandibulae internus (pseudotemporalis and pterygoideus)
occurrences.innervation: Mandibular ramus of the trigeminal nerve, the pterygoideus by the nervus musculi pterygoidei.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Sphenodon punctatus, Haas (1973), from his own dissections of two specimens — one from the Basel Museum and one from the British Museum (Natural History). **Two characters here are read as primitive and one is unique to the tuatara.** The pseudotemporalis has separate superficial and deep parts, which Haas takes as the primitive condition — shared with birds, amphisbaenians and most lizard families, while gekkonids, pygopodids and snakes retain only one. Superficialis from the posterior postorbital and anterolateral parietal to the medial face of the anteroventral basal aponeurosis; profundus a two-layered fleshy muscle lateral and anterior to the epipterygoid, its outer layer with two heads that the dorsal end of the epipterygoid sits between, inserting on the medial coronoid and anterior articular.

**M. pterygoideus atypicus has no counterpart in any squamate.** The typicus is the ordinary lizard muscle, forming the ventrally bulging masticatory cushion, from the ectopterygoid, both surfaces of the pterygoid, the ventrolateral epipterygoid and the pterygoid lamella of the quadrate, inserting by an internal tendon on the ventromedial ridge of the splenial with lateral fibres to the articular and medial ones to the angular. The atypicus arises far anterior to it, from the dorsal palatine and the ventral interorbital septum below the eye, and inserts on the coronoid region. **Only its innervation gives it away** — a branch of the nervus musculi pterygoidei is the sole evidence that this unique muscle derives from the typicus. Haas notes that birds and crocodylians have two superposed pterygoideus portions, turtles apparently only the dorsal one, and squamates only the ventral.

occurrences.name: M. adductor mandibulae internus
occurrences.innervation: Mandibular ramus of the trigeminal nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Agama stellio, Haas (1973), from his own dissection — his original figures 34, 35, 38 and 40. **Exceptionally well developed in agamids**, in Haas's words. The pseudotemporalis superficialis arises from the base of the postorbital bar and bulges into the anteromedial corner of the temporal fenestra, inserting bipinnately on the anterior division of the basal aponeurosis; the profundus is particularly large and entirely fleshy, arising not only from the anterodorsal and anteroventral prootic but from the lateral rim of the parietal in front of it.

occurrences.name: M. adductor mandibulae internus
occurrences.innervation: Mandibular ramus of the trigeminal nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Lanthanotus borneensis, Haas (1973), from his own dissection; he is the only reference for this animal in his own list of forms studied. **Two snake-like characters in a lizard.** The pseudotemporalis is well developed but its separation into superficial and deep portions is only weakly indicated — remove the superficial part gradually and no sharp plane appears — where most lizards and amphisbaenians have two clear heads and **all snakes have only one**. Its fibres run slightly posteroventrally rather than anteroventrally, and most of them insert directly on the lower jaw with only a few anterior ones reaching the basal aponeurosis. The pterygoideus has a normal portion forming a rather small masticatory cushion and a short-fibered posterodorsal portion **resembling the M. pterygoideus accessorius of several snake groups**.

occurrences.name: Pseudotemporalis + pterygoideus
occurrences.attachmentNote: *Grus americana*, Fisher & Goodman (1955); anconal and palmar are dorsal and ventral in their usage. **M. pseudotemporalis.** The origin is well depicted in figure 2; usually it is fleshy but in one instance aponeurotic origin was also found. Thus the insertion is covered medially by the insertion of the medial layer of M. add. mandib. medius. *Insertion.* —At the postero-ventral corner of the eye, the heavy belly gives way to a strong, flat, calcified tendon which goes ventrad super- ficial to the medial part of M. add. mandib. medius (fig. 5). The tendon inserts on the middle of the width of the mandible, about 3 centimeters from the posterior end of the bone. Thus the insertion is covered medially by the insertion of the medial layer of M. add. mandib. medius. **M. pterygoideus ventralis.** The superficial layer is overlaid anteriorly by a strong, silvery aponeurosis which forms part of the origin from the ventral area of the palatine, and particularly from the medial edge. Deep to this aponeurotic origin there is strong fleshy origin from the entire ventral concavity of the palatine. The lateral part of the deep sheet arises tendinously from the posterior half of the lateral corner of the palatal wing; the medial part of this layer comes fleshily from the posterior end of the palatine (fig. 7) and passes posteriorly over M. protract. pteryg. Insertion.—The superficial muscle attaches fleshily on the outer face of the posterior part of the mandible, on all that part of this *Insertion.* The superficial muscle attaches fleshily on the outer face of the posterior part of the mandible, on all that part of this bone covered by the muscle in figure 1. Medial to this insertion is a thin line of ten- dinous insertion going dorsad on the inner aspect of the mandible and between the origin of the lateral, deep fasciculus and the medial part of the insertion of M. depress. mandib. The lateral, deep fasciculus of M. pteryg. vent. inserts fleshily on the medial face of the mandible in an area delimited posteriorly by the in- sertion of M. depress. mandib., ventrally by the ventral edge of the man- dible, and dorsally in its anterior extent by the ventral edge of the lateral slip of **M. pterygoideus dorsalis.** The lateral part has tendinous and fleshy origin from the en- tire dorso-lateral surface of the palatine as far anterior as the most ante- rior part of the origin of the superficial layer of M. pteryg. vent. shown in 94 THE MYOLOGY OF THE WHOOPING CRANE figure 7. occurrences.name: M. adductor mandibulae externus
occurrences.innervation: Mandibular ramus of the trigeminal nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Sphenodon punctatus, Haas (1973), from his own dissections of two specimens — one from the Basel Museum and one from the British Museum (Natural History). Superficialis from the postorbital and squamosal along the anterior and dorsal margins of the lower temporal fenestra — the anterior half of the origin fleshy, the posterior half from a tendinous sheet that enlarges the area considerably — inserting on the angular and articular along the dorsolateral postcoronoid mandible and on the lateral face of the basal aponeurosis.

**The medialis has five heads and Haas is the first to say so.** Earlier descriptions he calls oversimplified: Poglayen-Neuwall gave one origin, Lakjer two. Haas resolves 2a (anteromedial, near-vertical fibres) and 2b (posterior, near-horizontal) converging on the anterior sheet of the basal aponeurosis as a bipinnate pair separated from 2c by an intervening blood vessel; 2c arises more ventrolaterally from the squamosal and inserts deeper; 2d and 2e are two small heads from the upper temporal arch that Poglayen-Neuwall had wrongly assigned to the superficialis. All five meet Lakjer's criterion by inserting on the lateral face of the aponeurosis. The profundus is bipinnate with two quite separate origins — the posterior wall of the dorsal temporal fenestra and the posterodorsal process of the prootic — and inserts on the aponeurosis's medial face.

occurrences.name: M. adductor mandibulae externus
occurrences.innervation: Mandibular ramus of the trigeminal nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Agama stellio, Haas (1973), from his own dissection — his original figures 34, 35, 38 and 40. The superficialis is divided into anterior and posterior parts; the medialis resembles that of *Calotes* in **failing to occupy the entire temporal fenestra**, so that in front of it the profundus rather than the pseudotemporalis superficialis is what gets exposed — a dissector's landmark stated as a taxonomic character. The profundus is separated from the medialis by the **temporal artery and vein** and fills the whole temporal fossa medial to it; heads 3a and 3b are fused, while 3c, arising from the quadrate, is well separated from both. A blood vessel doing the work a fascial plane does elsewhere.

occurrences.name: M. adductor mandibulae externus
occurrences.innervation: Mandibular ramus of the trigeminal nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Lanthanotus borneensis, Haas (1973), from his own dissection; he is the only reference for this animal in his own list of forms studied. **Why this animal is here: it is where two authors partition the same muscle mass differently.** *Lanthanotus* has a very elongate temporal region, no trace of a temporal arch and a widely open braincase, so the layers can be followed in a lizard built like a snake. Its medialis is very complicated and highly subdivided, arising from the temporal ridge, the entire anterior edge of the quadrate, and the temporal surfaces of the parietal and supratemporal wings — so the dorsal articulation of the quadrate does not mark the muscle's posterior end as it does in typical snakes. Most of the profundus lies well posteriorly and dorsally, even posttemporally.

The dorsal fibres reaching the basal aponeurosis from a posterodorsolateral position **belong to the profundus**, which the temporal vein separates from the medialis. Those fibres are the equivalent of what Lakjer (1926) called the M. adductor mandibulae externus medialis dorsalis in snakes — and on that basis **Haas argues Lakjer's muscle is not a distinct muscle at all**, but part of the profundus.

**That is a disagreement between two authors about how to divide one mass, and it is recorded here, not acted on.** Haas's claim is about *Lanthanotus*, which he dissected; Lakjer's was about snakes, which Haas did not dissect for this point. Nothing of Lakjer's is removed by this row — the dataset holds no Lakjer-derived snake rows, and if it did they would stand as their own species-and-source rows beside this one, with the disagreement in the `homology` notes. A row is an observation of one animal by one worker; it cannot delete another worker's observation of a different animal. The supratemporal is not an element in this skeleton, so that part of the origin is carried in prose rather than as a row — the same call made for the scapulosternal ligament in the *Iguana* costocoracoideus.

occurrences.name: M. compressor glandulae (M. adductor mandibulae externus superficialis)
occurrences.innervation: Mandibular ramus of the trigeminal nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Maticora sp., Haas (1973), from his own dissection of a very large specimen in the Field Museum, Chicago. **The venom gland is enclosed in a single, uninterrupted muscular loop**, and seeing that is what settles the muscle's identity. Radovanović (1935) missed the sac and therefore read the large steeply-fibred adductor medial to the Harderian gland as an abnormal superficialis; Haas assigns it instead to the **medialis**, on three grounds — its deep position, its remoteness from the postorbital, and its insertion medial to the laterally extended insertion of the profundus — while the superficial muscle looping the gland has the innervation typical of a superficialis.

The fibres originate from the postorbital and parietal ridge as in other snakes and stop at the capsule of the gland dorsally, posteriorly or even posteroventrally, forming a loop around its posterior margin; in some forms the dorsal fibres arise suborbitally from the back of the maxilla instead. The ventral part fans anterolaterally from the capsule to an elongate insertion on the lateral mandible. Haas reads *Pelamis* and *Lapemis* as more primitive because the muscle is not completely interrupted there, and argues from this that the proteroglyphs derive from colubrids that had already lost the levator anguli oris.

occurrences.attachmentNote: One to two heads arising anteromedially on the quadrate, medial to the adductor mandibulae externus; inserts partly directly and partly by its own tendon. Insertion on the articular puts it at the centre of the inverted U formed by the other components (Johnston 2011). Re-attributed from *Trachemys scripta*. occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae posterior
occurrences.attachmentNote: Columba livia. From the ventral part of the anterolateral surface of the quadrate, ventromedial to the origin of the externus pars profundus, onto a flat triangular surface on the dorsal mandible immediately anterior to the jaw joint. Jones et al. find it reasonably distinct from the externus pars profundus (contra van Gennip 1986) and clearly separate from the pseudotemporalis profundus. Its size and position suggest it stabilises the jaws during closure and may assist opening — a function no in vivo recording has tested.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae posterior

A cylindrical belly running from the anterior face of the quadrate to the dorsal mandible immediately rostral to the articulation. This is the axis the adductor sheet folds around, and Johnston's argument that it is of different homology from the rest of the group is what makes the remainder resolvable at all.

occurrences.name: Adductor mandibulae posterior
occurrences.attachmentNote: Alligator mississippiensis, Schumacher (1973). It shares the cranial adductor tendon with the externus — Iordansky's A- and B-tendons — anchored on the roof of the skull, so the two muscles are yoked at their origin as well as at their insertion.

occurrences.name: M. adductor mandibulae posterior
occurrences.innervation: Mandibular ramus of the trigeminal nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Sphenodon punctatus, Haas (1973), from his own dissections of two specimens — one from the Basel Museum and one from the British Museum (Natural History). This record holds the muscle Johnston treats as being of different homology from the rest of the adductor group — the axis the folded sheet wraps around — and the tuatara shows that axis only half detached.

occurrences.name: M. adductor mandibulae posterior

Since this record is defined by lying posterolateral to that nerve, a nerve that has moved takes the definition with it. occurrences.name: Levator anguli oris
occurrences.note: Newly defined in Ascaphus truei by Johnston (2011) — the first record of this muscle in a frog — and not found in Leiopelma hochstetteri, which now carries its own absent row. Presence was `variable` here for several passes, which was the clade's answer written onto one animal: Ascaphus either has the muscle or does not, and it has it.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Ascaphus truei. Arises from the dorsal surface of the palatal membrane in the triangular area between pterygoid and maxilla — the membrane is the actual origin and has no element, so the two bones bounding it are scored instead — wraps around the rostral border of the longus, and passes medial to the maxilla and the maxillo-quadrate ligament to insert on the rictal plate at the corner of the mouth. Johnston names it for the lepidosaur muscle because that insertion is the lepidosaur one; the same rictal plate is what becomes the venom gland in colubroid snakes on his 2014 reading.

occurrences.name: Levator anguli oris
occurrences.note: The most superficial layer of the typical lepidosaurian pattern, attaching to the rictal plate. McDowell (1986) identified the rostral 'external adductor' component of colubroid snakes as this muscle, modified around the venom gland — the second of the two moves reconciling lizard and snake anatomy.

Absent in Leiopelma hochstetteri. Johnston (2011) identifies the muscle in Ascaphus truei — the first record of a levator anguli oris in any frog — and does not find it in Leiopelma, so the two basal anuran lineages differ and Anura computes as variable rather than being declared so.

Homo sapiens, Gest (Anatomy Tables). **Absent, and the reason to say so is that a human has a muscle of this name which is not this muscle.** The record holds the lepidosaur levator anguli oris, a trigeminal jaw muscle whose identification is the crux of the lizard-snake problem — in colubroid snakes the rictal plate becomes the venom gland and parts of the muscle insert onto the gland or the mandible. Gest's levator anguli oris is a facial-expression muscle on the facial nerve, running from the maxilla to the corner of the mouth, and is scored as part of the `interhyoideus` field. Two muscles, one name, two different cranial nerves and two different arches.

occurrences.name: M. levator anguli oris and M. retractor anguli oris
occurrences.innervation: Mandibular ramus of the trigeminal nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote:
Sphenodon punctatus, Haas (1973), from his own dissections of two specimens — one from the Basel Museum and one from the British Museum (Natural History). **This record's homology note calls the muscle's identification the crux of the lizard–snake problem, and Haas's account is a four-way disagreement about whether it exists at all.** Lakjer (1926) overlooked it in *Sphenodon*. A. Luther, editing Lakjer's own paper, contradicted him in print, reporting both a levator and a retractor anguli oris and blaming a poorly preserved specimen. Poglayen-Neuwall (1953) figured one muscle, from the medial surface of the horizontal ramus of the jugal. Frazzetta likewise one. Haas's two dissections support Luther: two separate muscles, though the levator differed substantially between his Basel and London animals — and in the Basel specimen there are arguably **three**, counting a posterior steeply-fibred slip of the externus superficialis that also ends on the rictal area.

The levator arises from a limited area on the anteromedial postorbital near its postfrontal suture and inserts mostly on the medial surface of the medial rictal plate; the retractor mainly by tendon from the medial surface of the ventral squamosal and, in the London specimen, from adjacent quadratojugal and jugal — **not from the lower temporal arch proper in either animal**. Their insertions are completely separate.

**The comparative point is what makes the row worth having.** In *Sphenodon* the insertion is the same as in lizards but the origin has not shifted to the upper temporal arch, which Haas reads as the more primitive arrangement. And because crocodylians and birds lack the muscle entirely and have no adductor arising from the lower temporal arch, the tuatara is the only living animal with two temporal arches whose lower arch gives origin to any part of the adductor mandibulae complex.

occurrences.name: M. levator anguli oris and M. retractor anguli oris
occurrences.innervation: Mandibular ramus of the trigeminal nerve.
occurrences.attachmentNote: Agama stellio, Haas (1973), from his own dissection — his original figures 34, 35, 38 and 40. Both muscles are present and figured, with the retractor's tendon running superficial and parallel to the tendon on which the medialis inserts at the posterior margin of the coronoid. **This is the lizard end of the comparison Haas draws with *Sphenodon***: in the tuatara the insertion is already the lizard one but the origin has not yet shifted to the upper temporal arch, whereas in lizards it has. Note also the quadrato-maxillary ligament, which Haas figures repeatedly here and has to remove before the superficialis can be seen.

occurrences.note: Maticora sp., Haas (1973), from his own dissection of a very large specimen in the Field Museum, Chicago. **No trace of any M. levator anguli oris**, and the absence carries an argument. Haas's reading is that the proteroglyphous snakes descend from colubrids that had already lost this muscle, and that only after the centre of the semicircular adductor mandibulae externus 1b became attached to the venom gland capsule did the dorsal half differentiate further, as in *Dendroaspis*. So on this record — whose identification this dataset calls the crux of the lizard–snake problem — the snake end is an absence used as a phylogenetic character. Compare the *Sphenodon* row, where the muscle exists but four workers disagreed about whether it does.

homology.notes: Its identification is the crux of the lizard–snake problem. In colubroid snakes the rictal plate becomes the venom gland, so parts of the muscle insert on the gland or straight onto the mandible instead.
homology.openQuestion: Johnston (2014) notes that authors after McDowell (1986) neither adopted nor extended his model; the homology is endorsed here but is not consensus.
homology.teaching: A muscle whose insertion target itself evolved into a novel organ — the venom gland.
